q: A couple signs a written agreement with Dana under which Dana will be artificially inseminated, carry the child, and surrender custody at birth, in exchange for $25,000 described as compensation for “pain and suffering.” The state's adoption statute bars a birth mother from consenting to surrender a child until four days after the birth. Seven months into the pregnancy, Dana tells the couple she will keep the baby. The couple sues to enforce the agreement. How should the court rule?
o: For Dana: statute and public policy can override a bargain both sides assented to.
For the couple: both sides assented in a signed writing, and the $25,000 is consideration.
For the couple, but only for damages, since courts never order a child surrendered.
For Dana, because a surrogacy agreement lacks consideration.
oe: Correct. R.R. v. M.H.: a contract is a promise the law will remedy (R2d § 1). The pre-birth consent conflicted with the adoption statute, and the payment made the deal look like a sale of parental rights. Custody turns on the child's best interests, not the contract.
Assent and consideration are necessary but not sufficient. The law must also recognize the bargain, and here a statute and public policy override it.
The agreement isn't enforceable at all. Neither specific performance nor damages is available on a bargain the law won't recognize.
There was a bargained-for exchange. The problem is public policy and the adoption statute, not missing consideration.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Public policy overrides assent

q: Variation: Same facts. The court refuses to enforce the agreement, and both Dana and the husband (the genetic father) seek custody. What governs the custody decision?
o: The child's best interests, not the terms of the failed agreement.
The agreement's custody term, because the parties agreed to it in writing.
Automatic custody for the genetic father, because he provided the sperm.
Automatic custody for Dana, because the contract is void as against her.
oe: Correct. In R.R. v. M.H., once the agreement was unenforceable, custody turned on the child's best interests, as in any custody dispute.
The agreement is unenforceable, so its custody term has no force.
Genetics alone doesn't decide custody; best interests do.
Unenforceability doesn't award custody to either side; the court applies the best-interests standard.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Custody after refusal
pre: A couple signs a written agreement with Dana under which Dana will be artificially inseminated, carry the child, and surrender custody at birth, in exchange for $25,000 described as compensation for “pain and suffering.” The state's adoption statute bars a birth mother from consenting to surrender a child until four days after the birth. Seven months into the pregnancy, Dana tells the couple she will keep the baby. The couple sues to enforce the agreement. How should the court rule?

q: Riya, a junior staffer on a mayoral campaign, signs the campaign's form agreement. She promises never to disclose “any information the candidate or his family wish to remain private,” with no time limit, and never to disparage “the candidate, his family, or any entity he owns or may come to own.” After the election, Riya sues for a declaration that both provisions are unenforceable. The campaign asks the court, at a minimum, to narrow the clauses to a reasonable scope and enforce them as narrowed. What's the most likely result?
o: Both provisions are void as too vague, and the court won't rewrite them.
Both provisions are enforceable because Riya signed them and was paid for her work.
The court will narrow the provisions to information that is truly confidential and enforce them as narrowed.
Only the non-disparagement clause fails, because confidentiality clauses are always enforceable.
oe: Correct. Denson v. Donald J. Trump for President: terms must be definite enough for the promisor to know what's required and for a court to detect breach (R2d § 33). The court declined to blue-pencil the provisions.
A signature doesn't make an indefinite promise enforceable. The defect is that no one can tell what conduct the terms forbid.
That's blue-penciling, which the court in Denson declined to do. A court won't write a definite contract the parties didn't make.
Both clauses failed in Denson. The confidentiality definition reached essentially anything the candidate wanted kept private, with no time limit.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Vague NDA terms

q: Variation: Same facts, except the agreement defines confidential information as “the campaign's donor lists, internal polling data, and strategy memoranda,” lasts two years after the election, and bars disparaging only the campaign organization. Riya argues the provisions are void under Denson. What's the likely result?
o: They're likely enforceable: the terms are now definite.
They're void, because Denson held campaign NDAs unenforceable as a class.
They're void, because non-disparagement clauses always violate public policy.
They're enforceable only if a court first blue-pencils them.
oe: Correct. Denson turned on the open-ended, undefined scope. Specific categories, a time limit, and a defined target give a basis for determining breach and a remedy (R2d § 33).
Denson held these particular provisions too vague, not all NDAs.
The defect in Denson was indefiniteness, not a per se policy rule.
Nothing here needs rewriting; the terms are definite as drafted.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — A definite NDA

She promises never to disclose “any information the candidate or his family wish to remain private,” with no time limit, and never to disparage “the candidate, his family, or any entity he owns or may come to own.” After the election, Riya sues for a declaration that both provisions are unenforceable. The campaign asks the court, at a minimum, to narrow the clauses to a reasonable scope and enforce them as narrowed. What's the most likely result?

q: Gran tells her grandson Theo, “I'll give you $15,000 toward a car so you can take the job across town.” Gran wants nothing in return. Relying on the promise, Theo signs a lease on a car and accepts the job. Gran then refuses to pay, arguing that without a bargain there can't be a contract. What's Theo's best response?
o: Under R2d § 17(2), a contract can arise without a bargain under special rules such as § 90.
His acceptance of the job was consideration for Gran's promise.
Gran's promise is binding because a promise to a family member is presumed to be bargained for.
No response works: a promise without consideration is never enforceable.
oe: Correct. Formation ordinarily requires a bargain, mutual assent, and consideration (§ 17(1)), but § 17(2) recognizes contracts under §§ 82–94 without a bargain, including promissory estoppel (§ 90) for foreseeable, induced reliance.
Gran didn't seek the job in exchange for her promise. Without that, there's no bargain (§ 71).
There's no such presumption. Family promises are often gifts.
Section 90 is the standard exception, and § 17(2) expressly preserves it.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Contract without a bargain

q: For two summers, Marco's lawn service mowed Eleanor's lawn every Monday. Each time, Eleanor left $60 in an envelope on her porch. They never discussed terms. In August, after four more mowings, Eleanor stops leaving envelopes and refuses to pay, arguing they never made a contract because she never promised anything. Which is the best characterization?
o: An implied-in-fact contract, as enforceable as an express one.
No contract, because a promise must be stated in words, oral or written.
A quasi-contract, because there was no express agreement.
No contract, but Marco may recover the reasonable value of the mowings as restitution.
oe: Correct. R2d § 4: a promise may be stated in words or inferred wholly or partly from conduct. The course of conduct shows a promise to pay $60 per mowing, and expectation damages are available.
Section 4 expressly allows a promise to be inferred from conduct.
Quasi-contract is not a contract at all. It's a restitution remedy where there was no assent. Here the conduct shows real assent.
Restitution is a fallback when there's no contract. The parties' conduct is a manifestation of mutual assent, so there's a real contract (§ 3).
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Implied-in-fact contract

q: Dr. Patel comes upon an unconscious motorist after a crash and gives emergency treatment that saves his life. The motorist never regains consciousness during the treatment and never asks for help. Dr. Patel later sends a bill for her usual fee. The motorist refuses to pay, arguing he never agreed to anything. Which is most accurate?
o: There's no contract, but she may recover restitution measured by the benefit conferred.
There's an implied-in-fact contract, so she recovers her usual fee as expectation damages.
She can't recover anything, because there was no offer or acceptance.
There's an express contract, because emergency treatment implies the patient's promise to pay.
oe: Correct. This is implied-in-law (quasi-contract): not a contract, but a remedy imposed to prevent unjust enrichment, measured by the benefit conferred.
An implied-in-fact contract needs a real manifestation of assent through conduct. An unconscious person manifests nothing.
The lack of a contract doesn't end the analysis. Restitution can prevent unjust enrichment without assent.
Nothing was stated, so nothing was express. If anything were implied from conduct, it would be implied-in-fact, but there was no conduct by the motorist.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Quasi-contract

q: A builder sues a homeowner for the unpaid $40,000 balance of a construction contract. The complaint alleges (1) a valid written contract, (2) the homeowner's failure to pay the balance when due, and (3) $40,000 in damages. The homeowner moves to dismiss for failure to state a claim. On what ground is the motion most likely to succeed?
o: The complaint doesn't allege the builder's own performance or tender.
The complaint doesn't allege that the homeowner intended to breach.
The complaint doesn't allege that the contract was supported by a writing signed by the builder.
The complaint must allege the homeowner's subjective agreement to the contract terms.
oe: Correct. A breach claim requires (1) a valid contract, (2) the plaintiff's performance or tender, (3) the defendant's breach, and (4) damages. The complaint omits the second element.
Intent to breach isn't an element. Breach is a failure to perform when due.
The Statute of Frauds is a defense, not an element the plaintiff must plead.
Assent is judged objectively, and a valid contract is already alleged.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Elements of a breach claim

q: Harbor Industries signs four contracts in one week. Which one is governed by UCC Article 2?
o: A contract for a printing press built to Harbor's design.
A contract to buy 2,000 shares of a listed company's stock.
A contract to buy a warehouse and the land under it.
A two-year contract hiring a plant manager.
oe: Correct. Goods include specially manufactured goods, things movable at identification to the contract (§ 2-105(1)).
Investment securities are excluded from goods.
Land and real-estate interests go to the common law.
Employment contracts are governed by the common law, with the Restatement as persuasive authority.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — What counts as goods

q: Variation: Same facts, except Harbor's affiliate, a ranch, contracts to sell next spring's calves from its herd (not yet born) and the wheat now growing in its fields. Do these contracts involve goods?
o: Yes, both: the statute expressly lists unborn young and growing crops as goods.
Only the wheat: animals not yet born can't be identified to a contract.
Only the calves: crops still attached to land are part of the realty.
Neither: goods must exist and be movable when the contract is made.
oe: Correct. Section 2-105(1) expressly includes the unborn young of animals and growing crops.
Section 2-105(1) expressly lists unborn young as goods.
Growing crops are expressly goods under § 2-105(1).
The test is movability at the time of identification to the contract, and the statute expressly includes both categories.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Unborn young and growing crops
pre: Harbor Industries signs four contracts in one week. Which one is governed by UCC Article 2?

q: A collector buys a rare 1916 dime from a coin shop for $900, paying with ten $100 bills. Separately, she buys a court judgment worth $5,000 from a creditor for $3,000. Which, if either, is a transaction in goods?
o: Only the coin: it's the thing sold, while the judgment is a thing in action.
Both, because each involves a transfer of property for a price.
Neither, because money and money-related rights are never goods.
Only the judgment purchase, because the coin is money.
oe: Correct. Only money used to pay the price is excluded; a collectible coin sold as a commodity is a good. A judgment is a thing in action (an intangible right), which is excluded (§ 2-105(1)).
A judgment is a thing in action, excluded from goods.
The exclusion reaches the money in which the price is paid, not a coin that is itself the thing sold.
The coin is the subject of the sale, not the price. The bills she paid with are the excluded money.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Things in action and the price

q: A restaurant contracts with Kitchenworks for a new commercial kitchen for $50,000: $44,000 for ovens, refrigerators, and ranges, and $6,000 to install them over two days. A dispute arises over whether the parties ever formed a contract. Which law most likely governs?
o: UCC Article 2, because the deal's essence is the sale of equipment.
The common law, because the contract includes services.
Article 2 for the equipment and the common law for the installation, applied separately.
The common law, because the buyer is a restaurant, not a merchant in kitchens.
oe: Correct. Most courts apply the predominant-purpose test to mixed contracts. Here the equipment is the heart of the deal, and installation is incidental.
Including some services doesn't move a contract out of Article 2. The question is which predominates.
The predominant-purpose test classifies the whole contract by its essence rather than splitting it.
Merchant status doesn't decide which law governs. Article 2 applies to transactions in goods regardless.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Predominant purpose

q: Variation: Same facts, except the contract is a $50,000 three-year agreement under which Kitchenworks will design the restaurant's workflow, train staff, and provide monthly maintenance, and supply $3,000 of small utensils. Which law most likely governs?
o: The common law, because the essence of the deal is services.
Article 2, because any transfer of goods brings the whole contract within the UCC.
Article 2, because Kitchenworks is a merchant.
Neither, because mixed contracts can't be enforced until the parties allocate the price.
oe: Correct. Under the predominant-purpose test, design, training, and maintenance dominate; the utensils are incidental.
The test asks what predominates, not whether any goods are involved.
Merchant status doesn't determine scope.
Mixed contracts are enforceable. Courts classify them by their predominant purpose.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Services predominate
pre: A restaurant contracts with Kitchenworks for a new commercial kitchen for $50,000: $44,000 for ovens, refrigerators, and ranges, and $6,000 to install them over two days. A dispute arises over whether the parties ever formed a contract. Which law most likely governs?

q: Celia, a retired teacher, inherited a painting. She hires a professional art dealer as her broker to sell it to a gallery. A dispute arises over whether a rule that applies only to merchants governs the sale. Could Celia be treated as a merchant?
o: Yes: a broker's skill can be attributed to her.
No: only a person who regularly deals in goods of the kind can be a merchant.
No: a retired person can never be a merchant.
Yes, because any seller of goods worth more than $500 is a merchant.
oe: Correct. Section 2-104(1) includes a person to whom knowledge or skill peculiar to the goods or practices is attributable through an agent or broker who holds himself out as having it.
Dealing in goods of the kind is one route. Holding oneself out by occupation, or skill attributable through an agent or broker, are others.
Status turns on dealing, holding out, or attributed skill, not employment status.
The $500 figure belongs to the Statute of Frauds, not the merchant definition.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Merchant through a broker

q: Ana, a nurse, sends her neighbor Ben, an accountant, a signed letter: “I'll sell you my piano for $3,000. This offer is firm until June 1.” Ben pays nothing for the promise. On May 1, Ana calls Ben and withdraws the offer. On May 2, Ben writes back accepting. Is there a contract?
o: No: the § 2-205 firm-offer rule requires a merchant, so Ana's offer was revocable.
Yes: an offer in a signed writing with an assurance it will be held open is irrevocable.
Yes: the piano is a good, so Article 2 makes every written offer irrevocable for a reasonable time.
No, because the piano costs more than $500 and Ben's acceptance wasn't signed by Ana.
oe: Correct. Firm offers are one of the merchant-only rules. A non-merchant's written promise to hold an offer open is revocable unless § 87(1) applies, and this letter recites no consideration.
That's § 2-205, but it applies only to an offer by a merchant.
Article 2 applies, but the firm-offer rule within it is limited to merchants.
Ana's signed letter could satisfy the Statute of Frauds anyway. The point is that the offer was revoked before acceptance.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Merchant-only rules

q: At a staff meeting, a company president says: “We intend to give everyone a 10% raise next year if things keep going well.” Business stays strong, but no raises come. An employee sues for breach. What's the president's best defense?
o: The statement expressed an intention, not a commitment.
There was no consideration because the employees did nothing new.
Oral promises of raises are unenforceable under the Statute of Frauds.
The president lacked authority to bind the company.
oe: Correct. A promise (R2d § 2) is a manifestation of intention to act made so as to justify the promisee in understanding that a commitment has been made. “We intend … if things keep going well” describes plans, not a commitment.
Consideration would matter only if there were a promise to support.
The Statute of Frauds isn't the problem. The threshold problem is that there's no promise.
Nothing suggests that; the better defense is that no promise was made.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Statement of intention vs. promise

q: On May 1, a buyer sues a seller for failing to deliver a custom boat. The contract requires delivery by June 1. The complaint alleges a valid contract, the buyer's payment of the deposit, and damages from a lost charter booking. The seller moves to dismiss. What's the strongest ground?
o: No breach is alleged, because the seller's performance isn't yet due.
The buyer hasn't tendered the full price.
A boat is a good, so the claim must be brought under the UCC rather than as a breach of contract.
The damages are too speculative.
oe: Correct. A breach claim needs a valid contract, the plaintiff's performance or tender, the defendant's breach, and damages. Failing to deliver before the June 1 deadline isn't a breach.
The buyer alleges its own performance to date (the deposit). The missing element is a breach.
A UCC claim is still a breach-of-contract claim with the same core elements.
The more basic defect is that no duty has been breached yet.
topic: Wk 1 · Enforceable agreements & governing law — Breach requires a duty that's due

q: After several beers at a marina bar, Owen tells Pia he'd sell her his sailboat for $20,000. They talk about it for half an hour. Pia asks him to put it in writing. Owen writes “I agree to sell my boat Windward to Pia for $20,000” on a napkin, crosses out and rewrites a word, and signs. Pia arranges a loan the next week. Owen then says he was joking the whole time and secretly never meant to sell. Pia sues for specific performance. What result?
o: Pia wins: Owen's words and acts objectively showed serious assent.
Owen wins, because he never subjectively intended to sell.
Owen wins, because agreements made in a bar are presumed to be jokes.
Pia wins only if Owen was completely sober when he signed.
oe: Correct. Lucy v. Zehmer: assent is judged by outward manifestations as a reasonable person in Pia's position would understand them. A secret, unexpressed jest is no defense.
Undisclosed subjective intent is irrelevant under the objective theory (R2d §§ 17–19).
There's no such presumption. The question is how a reasonable person would read the conduct, and here it showed seriousness.
Intoxication matters only if it destroyed capacity and Pia had reason to know it (§ 16).
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Secret jest

q: Variation: Same facts, except that just before Owen wrote on the napkin, he winked at Pia and said, “This'll be a great prop for my prank on my brother. Play along.” Pia laughed and said, “Sure.” Is there a contract?
o: No: Pia knew the statement wasn't serious.
Yes: the signed writing controls over anything said before it.
Yes: a secret jest is never a defense.
No, because a napkin isn't a sufficient writing for a boat.
oe: Correct. The jest doctrine protects only reasonable reliance. Pia knew it was a prank, so a reasonable person in her position wouldn't understand Owen to be assenting.
The objective test looks at all the circumstances known to Pia, including Owen's statement that it was a prank.
This jest wasn't secret. Owen disclosed it, so the objective meaning changes.
The issue is assent, not the form of the writing.

q: Rafe signs a contract selling his vintage motorcycle to Lena for $4,000. Lena had seen him drink most of a bottle of whiskey; he was slurring, couldn't stand without help, and she had to steady his hand to sign. The next morning Rafe says he doesn't remember signing and refuses to deliver. What's the best analysis?
o: The contract is voidable by Rafe, because Lena had reason to know he couldn't understand the deal.
The contract is void, because an intoxicated person can never manifest assent.
The contract is enforceable, because voluntary intoxication is never a defense.
The contract is enforceable, because Rafe's subjective failure to remember is irrelevant under the objective theory.
oe: Correct. R2d § 16: intoxication makes a contract voidable only if the other party has reason to know the intoxicated person can't understand the transaction or act reasonably. Lena saw the signs.
Intoxication at most makes the contract voidable, and only when the other party had reason to know.
Section 16 allows avoidance when the other party had reason to know of the incapacity.
Memory isn't the point. Capacity is, and Lena had reason to know he lacked it.
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Intoxication

q: Variation: Same facts, except Rafe had a few drinks but discussed the price for 40 minutes, negotiated $500 off, corrected a mistake in the description, and drove Lena to the bank afterward. He now says he was “feeling pretty good” and wouldn't have signed sober. What result?
o: The contract is enforceable: being merely high isn't incapacity.
Voidable, because any intoxication at signing lets the drinker avoid the contract.
Void, because he wouldn't have signed sober.
Voidable, but only if Lena bought him the drinks.
oe: Correct. Lucy v. Zehmer: Zehmer wasn't too drunk to know what he was doing, and the detailed negotiation shows understanding. Rafe's regret doesn't make the contract voidable.
Section 16 requires incapacity that the other party had reason to know of.
What he would have done sober isn't the test.
Who bought the drinks is irrelevant. The question is incapacity plus reason to know.
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Merely high

Lena had seen him drink most of a bottle of whiskey; he was slurring, couldn't stand without help, and she had to steady his hand to sign. q: On a cable news show, a defense attorney says of the prosecution's theory, “It's physically impossible for anyone to get from the office to the marina in 20 minutes. I'll pay a million dollars to anyone who can do it!” A viewer drives the route in 19 minutes at 3 a.m., films it, and sues for $1 million. What's the strongest defense?
o: It was hyperbole, not a serious offer.
The statement wasn't in writing.
The attorney never subjectively intended to pay.
The viewer gave no consideration.
oe: Correct. Kolodziej v. Mason: zealous advocacy in a televised interview is rhetorical hyperbole, not a serious offer. The objective test defeats the claim.
Offers needn't be written. The problem is that there was no offer.
Subjective intent is irrelevant. The defense works because the statement objectively wasn't an offer.
If it were a unilateral offer, performing the act would be the consideration. The real defense is that there was no offer.
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Rhetorical challenge

q: Variation: Same facts, and assume a court found the statement could be an offer. The attorney was arguing that the drive was impossible during the 5 p.m. rush hour, when the prosecution said the crime occurred, and said so in the same interview. Does the 3 a.m. drive accept?
o: No: he performed a different act from the one the offer actually described.
Yes: the offer said “anyone who can do it,” and he did it.
Yes: any ambiguity in an offer is construed against the offeror.
No, because he didn't notify the attorney before starting the drive.
oe: Correct. Kolodziej also held the student didn't perform the act Mason actually described. An offer can be accepted only by the performance it invites.
“It” referred to the drive under the conditions the attorney was disputing, which a reasonable listener would understand.
There was no real ambiguity in context, and the act performed wasn't the one invited.
Notice isn't required for acceptance by performance unless the offer requests it (§ 54(1)). The problem is that the act was different.
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Performing a different act
pre: On a cable news show, a defense attorney says of the prosecution's theory, “It's physically impossible for anyone to get from the office to the marina in 20 minutes. I'll pay a million dollars to anyone who can do it!” A viewer drives the route in 19 minutes at 3 a.m., films it, and sues for $1 million. What's the strongest defense?

q: At an art auction, Bram is reaching for his coffee when a passing server bumps his elbow, and his arm, holding his bidding paddle, flies up. The auctioneer calls “Sold!” at $30,000. Bram immediately protests. Is Bram bound?
o: No: conduct is assent only if the party intends to engage in it.
Yes: the auctioneer reasonably believed he was bidding, and assent is judged objectively.
Yes: a bidder bears the risk of any raised paddle.
No, because auction bids must be in writing.
oe: Correct. R2d § 19(2): conduct is not effective as a manifestation of assent unless the party intends to engage in the conduct and knows or has reason to know the other may infer assent. Bram didn't intend to raise his arm.
The objective theory applies to conduct the actor intends. Section 19 excludes conduct he didn't intend at all.
No such rule exists; § 19 governs.
Bids needn't be written. The problem is the lack of intended conduct.
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Unintended conduct

q: Variation: Same facts, except Bram deliberately raises his paddle high to wave to a friend across the room, knowing that raised paddles are how bids are made at this auction. What result?
o: Likely bound: he meant to raise the paddle and knew how bids are signaled.
Bram isn't bound, because he subjectively meant only to wave.
Bram isn't bound, because a wave can never be an acceptance.
Bram is bound only if he also says the amount aloud.
oe: Correct. Under § 19(2) both conditions are met, and his undisclosed purpose (waving) is irrelevant under the objective theory.
Undisclosed intent doesn't control. What matters is what he had reason to know the auctioneer would infer.
Conduct can be assent when § 19's conditions are met.
Words aren't required; conduct can manifest assent.
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Intended conduct, unintended meaning
pre: At an art auction, Bram is reaching for his coffee when a passing server bumps his elbow, and his arm, holding his bidding paddle, flies up. The auctioneer calls “Sold!” at $30,000. Bram immediately protests. Is Bram bound?

q: A private music conservatory's catalog features practice rooms and in-person lessons, it historically taught only in person, and it charges $40,000 for its residential program but $12,000 for a separate online program. After a flood closes the campus, it teaches the residential students online all semester and refuses any refund. The enrollment agreement says nothing about in-person instruction. Students sue. Which claim is most likely to survive a motion to dismiss?
o: Breach of an implied-in-fact promise of in-person instruction.
Breach of an express promise of in-person instruction.
None, because without a written promise of in-person instruction there's no contract term to breach.
Only unjust enrichment, because implied terms can't be added to a written enrollment agreement.
oe: Correct. Shaffer v. George Washington University: catalogs, historical practice, and separately priced online programs can plausibly show an implied promise (R2d § 4). The students may also plead unjust enrichment in the alternative.
No document expressly promised in-person instruction. In Shaffer the express-promise claims were dismissed.
Promises may be inferred from conduct and circumstances. That's what an implied-in-fact contract is.
The implied-contract claim survived in Shaffer, and unjust enrichment was pleaded in the alternative.
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Implied promise of in-person instruction

q: Variation: Same facts. At trial, the students prove the implied-in-fact contract claim. How is their recovery measured, compared with what they'd get if they proved only unjust enrichment?
o: Contract: expectation. Unjust enrichment: restitution of the benefit.
Both are measured by restitution, because the promise was implied rather than express.
Both are measured by expectation, because both are contracts.
Contract: restitution. Unjust enrichment: expectation.
oe: Correct. An implied-in-fact contract rests on real assent and gives expectation damages. Unjust enrichment has no assent and gives restitution measured by the benefit conferred.
Implied-in-fact contracts are real contracts with ordinary contract remedies.
Unjust enrichment (implied-in-law) isn't a contract; it's a restitution remedy.
That reverses the measures.
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Remedy difference
pre: A private music conservatory's catalog features practice rooms and in-person lessons, it historically taught only in person, and it charges $40,000 for its residential program but $12,000 for a separate online program. After a flood closes the campus, it teaches the residential students online all semester and refuses any refund. The enrollment agreement says nothing about in-person instruction. Students sue. Which claim is most likely to survive a motion to dismiss?

q: Variation: Same facts. The conservatory moves to dismiss the unjust-enrichment count, arguing that students can't claim a contract and unjust enrichment at the same time. What's the likely ruling?
o: Denied: students may plead unjust enrichment in the alternative.
Granted: an implied-in-fact contract and unjust enrichment are the same claim.
Granted: a plaintiff must elect one theory in the complaint.
Denied, because unjust enrichment always gives the larger recovery.
oe: Correct. In Shaffer, the unjust-enrichment claims were pleaded in the alternative and survived along with the implied-contract claims. If no contract is found, restitution remains available.
They differ: one rests on real assent and gives expectation; the other has no assent and gives restitution.
Alternative pleading is permitted.
The ruling doesn't depend on which recovery is larger.
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Pleading both theories
pre: A private music conservatory's catalog features practice rooms and in-person lessons, it historically taught only in person, and it charges $40,000 for its residential program but $12,000 for a separate online program. After a flood closes the campus, it teaches the residential students online all semester and refuses any refund. The enrollment agreement says nothing about in-person instruction. Students sue. Which claim is most likely to survive a motion to dismiss?

q: A software company emails Juno a signed offer letter: “We offer you the senior engineer position at $160,000 per year, starting March 1. Please sign and return by Friday.” Juno signs and returns it Thursday. The company's CEO later testifies that she sent the letter only to “gauge interest” and never meant it as a real offer. Is there a contract?
o: Yes: a reasonable person in Juno's position would read the letter as an offer.
No, because the company didn't subjectively intend to be bound.
No, because employment offers are always preliminary negotiations.
Yes, but only if Juno relied by quitting her old job.
oe: Correct. The objective theory looks to outward manifestations. The CEO's undisclosed intent to “gauge interest” is irrelevant (R2d §§ 17–19).
Undisclosed intent doesn't count.
A definite offer letter inviting a signature is an offer, not a preliminary negotiation.
Reliance isn't needed when there's offer, acceptance, and consideration.
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Undisclosed intent in an offer letter

q: On a radio call-in show the night before a rivalry game, a college coach says: “If we lose tomorrow, I'll buy every fan in the stadium a steak dinner!” His team loses. A fan who attended sues for a steak dinner. What result?
o: The fan loses: a reasonable listener would hear rhetorical bravado, not an offer.
The fan wins: the coach's statement was a unilateral offer accepted by attending.
The fan wins, because the coach subjectively meant it as a promise.
The fan loses only because a steak dinner isn't consideration.
oe: Correct. Hyperbole, boasts, and rhetorical challenges aren't offers because no reasonable person would understand them as inviting acceptance (compare Kolodziej).
A unilateral offer must be one a reasonable person would take seriously.
The facts don't say so, and the objective meaning controls anyway.
Consideration isn't the issue; there was no offer.
topic: Wk 2 · Objective assent & implied-in-fact contracts — Locker-room boast

q: A hardware store runs a newspaper ad: “Spring Sale! Riding mowers from $899. See our full selection.” Kai comes in the first morning, points to a mower tagged $899, and says, “I accept your offer.” The store says the sale price applied only to a floor model that has just sold and refuses to sell another at $899. Does Kai have a contract?
o: No: the ad was an invitation to deal, and Kai's statement was at most an offer.
Yes: an advertised price is an offer to anyone who accepts first.
Yes: the store's refusal is bait-and-switch, which forms a contract as a matter of law.
No, because a contract for goods over $500 must be in writing.
oe: Correct. Ads are generally invitations to deal, not offers. This one left quantity and other terms open, so it didn't justify Kai in thinking his assent would close a deal (R2d § 24).
Only an ad that is clear, definite, and explicit, leaving nothing open, is an offer.
Consumer-protection statutes might apply, but they don't turn an invitation into an offer under contract law.
$899 is over $500, but the threshold problem is that there was no offer to accept.
topic: Wks 2–3 · The offer — Newspaper ad

q: Variation: Same facts, except the ad says: “Saturday 9 a.m. sharp! 1 Brand-new riding mower, list price $2,400, for $99. First come, first served.” Kai is first in line at 9 a.m. and tenders $99. The store refuses. What result?
o: Kai has a contract: the ad was clear, definite, explicit, and left nothing open.
No contract: ads are never offers.
No contract: a $99 price for a $2,400 mower shows the store couldn't have been serious.
Kai has a contract only if he had already notified the store he would come.
oe: Correct. An ad is an offer when it states the quantity, the price, and who may accept (here, the first person), so nothing is left to negotiate.
Ads are generally invitations, but not always. This one is specific enough to be an offer.
Loss-leader sales are common, and the definite terms show seriousness.
The ad invited acceptance by showing up first, not by advance notice.
topic: Wks 2–3 · The offer — Definite ad
pre: A hardware store runs a newspaper ad: “Spring Sale! Riding mowers from $899. See our full selection.” Kai comes in the first morning, points to a mower tagged $899, and says, “I accept your offer.” The store says the sale price applied only to a floor model that has just sold and refuses to sell another at $899. Does Kai have a contract?

q: Steelco mails a brochure to construction firms: “Current price for Grade A rebar: $780/ton. Prices subject to change without notice. Contact our sales office to discuss your project.” Builder Corp. mails Steelco a purchase order for 200 tons at $780/ton. Before Steelco responds, steel prices jump, and Steelco declines the order. Is Steelco bound?
o: No: the brochure invited offers; Builder's order was the offer.
Yes: the brochure stated a definite price, so it was an offer Builder accepted.
Yes: a merchant's quotation is a firm offer under § 2-205.
No, because Builder's purchase order wasn't signed by Steelco.
oe: Correct. Price quotations are generally invitations to submit offers, and the buyer's purchase order is usually the offer. Here the reservation of price changes and the invitation to discuss confirm it.
A price alone isn't enough. The brochure lacked quantity, reserved changes to price, and invited further negotiation.
A firm offer requires a signed writing with assurance it will be held open. This one said the opposite.
The question is offer and acceptance, not the Statute of Frauds.
topic: Wks 2–3 · The offer — Price quotation

q: Variation: Same facts, except Builder had sent Steelco a request for a quote for 200 tons delivered June 1. Steelco replied with a signed quote: “200 tons Grade A rebar, $780/ton, delivered June 1 to your site, net 30. To accept, sign below and return.” Builder signs and returns it the next day. Is Steelco bound?
o: Yes: this quote was a definite offer.
No: quotations are never offers.
No, because Steelco reserved the right to approve the order.
Yes, but only because Steelco is a merchant.
oe: Correct. Those are the signs a quote is an offer. Builder's signature accepted it.
Quotes are generally invitations, but a detailed, unconditional quote responding to a request can be an offer.
Nothing in this quote reserves approval. It invites acceptance by signature.
Merchant status doesn't decide whether a communication is an offer.
topic: Wks 2–3 · The offer — Quote as an offer
pre: Steelco mails a brochure to construction firms: “Current price for Grade A rebar: $780/ton. Prices subject to change without notice. Contact our sales office to discuss your project.” Builder Corp. mails Steelco a purchase order for 200 tons at $780/ton. Before Steelco responds, steel prices jump, and Steelco declines the order. Is Steelco bound?

q: A salesman for SolarPro visits Nora's home. She signs SolarPro's form ordering a $28,000 solar array. The form states: “This order is subject to approval by SolarPro's home office.” Two days later, before SolarPro has approved, Nora calls SolarPro's office and cancels. SolarPro approves the order the next day and sues for breach. What result?
o: No contract: Nora's signed order was the offer, and she revoked it before acceptance.
Contract: SolarPro made the offer and Nora accepted when she signed.
Contract: SolarPro had a reasonable time to approve, and Nora couldn't cancel during it.
No contract, because a solar installation is a service, so no writing was signed by SolarPro.
oe: Correct. With a home-office approval clause, the seller has reserved the final say, so the seller's form isn't an offer; the buyer's order is. An offer is revocable until accepted.
The approval clause shows SolarPro didn't intend to be bound by Nora's signature alone.
Nothing made Nora's offer irrevocable. A reasonable time to accept doesn't block revocation.
The analysis turns on offer, revocation, and acceptance, not on the governing law or a writing.
topic: Wks 2–3 · The offer — Home-office approval clause

q: Mateo advertises a lakeside cabin for sale. Isla writes asking about it. Mateo replies: “This is a form letter going to everyone who asked. My lowest price is $210,000. I expect a buyer within the week, so if you are interested, I would suggest you act quickly.” Isla immediately mails back, “I accept your offer at $210,000.” Meanwhile Mateo had already signed a contract with another buyer. Does Isla have a contract?
o: No: Mateo's letter was preliminary negotiation, not an offer.
Yes: the letter stated a price and invited a prompt response.
Yes, because Isla's acceptance was effective on dispatch under the mailbox rule.
No, but only because Mateo's sale to another buyer revoked the offer.
oe: Correct. Lonergan v. Scolnick: “form letter,” “if you are interested,” and “act quickly” signal an invitation to deal. Isla had reason to know Mateo intended a further manifestation of assent (R2d § 26).
A price and a nudge to hurry don't create a power of acceptance where the language shows no intent to be bound.
The mailbox rule applies only to acceptances of offers. There was no offer.
The court in Lonergan said the sale would defeat the claim even if there had been an offer, but the primary reason is that there was no offer.
topic: Wks 2–3 · The offer — Preliminary negotiations

q: Gearworks emails Mill Co. a proposal for a $900,000 turbine, with “commercial terms” including a Texas forum clause and the statement “All offers and resulting orders are subject to Gearworks' board approval.” The same day, Mill Co. sends a purchase order that expressly excludes Gearworks' proposal terms. Gearworks immediately starts engineering work and promises a ship date. Later it sends an order confirmation attaching its terms. Mill Co., which isn't a merchant in turbines, makes milestone payments. The turbine never arrives, and Mill Co. sues at home. Is the Texas forum clause part of the contract?
o: No: Mill Co.'s order was the offer, and it never assented to the clause.
Yes: Gearworks' proposal was the offer, and Mill Co. accepted it with its purchase order.
Yes: making milestone payments after receiving the confirmation was assent to its terms.
No, because forum clauses are unenforceable in sales of goods.
oe: Correct. Eureka Resources v. Howden Roots: the board-approval proposal wasn't an offer. Gearworks accepted under § 2-206 by promptly beginning performance. Because Mill Co. isn't a merchant, the later terms were proposals under § 2-207(2), and making payments isn't express assent.
The board-approval clause and reserved terms meant Gearworks' proposal wasn't an offer.
Payment is performance, not express assent to new terms.
Forum clauses can be enforced if they're part of the contract. This one never became part of it.
topic: Wks 2–3 · The offer — Board approval and acceptance by performance

q: Supplier and Bakery negotiate for weeks over a flour-supply deal, exchanging drafts that are never signed. Neither can later identify which document was the offer or when the deal closed. For the next year, Supplier delivers flour every week, and Bakery pays each invoice at the drafts' common price. Supplier then stops delivering, and Bakery sues. Supplier argues there was never a contract because no offer was ever accepted. What result?
o: A contract exists: one can form without an identifiable offer and acceptance.
No contract: formation always requires an identifiable offer and acceptance.
No contract: unsigned drafts show the parties didn't intend to be bound.
A contract, but only for flour already delivered and paid for.
oe: Correct. R2d § 22(2) and UCC § 2-204(2) recognize this. Under § 2-204(1), conduct by both parties recognizing a contract is enough for goods.
Offer and acceptance is the ordinary mode of assent, not the only one (§ 22).
The year of performance shows they did. The lack of a signed draft isn't fatal.
The conduct may show a continuing agreement, not just past sales. The scope is a question of what the parties' conduct shows.
topic: Wks 2–3 · The offer — No identifiable offer and acceptance

q: On Monday, Vera emails Nate a definite offer to sell her used car for $8,000, “open until Friday.” On Tuesday, Vera privately decides she'd rather keep the car and tells her sister, but says nothing to Nate. On Wednesday, Nate emails Vera, “I accept.” Is there a contract?
o: Yes: nothing had terminated Nate's power of acceptance.
No: Vera revoked when she decided not to sell.
No: telling her sister was an indirect revocation.
Yes, but only because Vera promised to keep the offer open until Friday.
oe: Correct. An offer creates a continuing power of acceptance (§ 35(1)). Revocation is effective only when the offeree receives it (§ 42), and Vera's private change of mind wasn't communicated.
A revocation must be a manifestation received by the offeree.
Indirect revocation requires definite action inconsistent with the offer and reliable information reaching the offeree (§ 43). Nate learned nothing.
The promise didn't make the offer irrevocable (no consideration). It simply hadn't been revoked.
topic: Wks 2–3 · The offer — Continuing power of acceptance

q: A collector emails a dealer: “I might part with my 1952 Mantle card. I'd consider offers around $50,000. Let me know if you're interested and we can talk.” The dealer replies, “I accept at $50,000.” The collector sells to someone else. The dealer sues. What result?
o: No contract: the email only invited offers and further talks.
A contract at $50,000, because the email named a price.
A contract, because the dealer's acceptance was immediate.
No contract, because sports cards over $500 require a signed writing.
oe: Correct. Under R2d § 26, a manifestation isn't an offer if the addressee knows or has reason to know the sender won't conclude a bargain until a further manifestation of assent. As in Lonergan, “if you're interested” language signals negotiation.
A price figure doesn't turn an invitation to negotiate into an offer.
There was no offer to accept, however fast the reply.
The threshold problem is that there was no offer.
topic: Wks 2–3 · The offer — “Let me know if you're interested”

q: A hospital and a software consultant exchange drafts of a support agreement for months without signing. Meanwhile, the consultant answers the hospital's support calls and sends monthly invoices at the drafts' agreed rate, and the hospital pays them for a year. When the hospital refuses to pay for the final two months, it argues no contract was ever formed because no offer was ever accepted. What result?
o: A contract exists under § 22(2), formed by the parties' conduct.
No contract: services contracts require an identifiable offer and acceptance.
No contract, but the consultant may recover the reasonable value of the services.
A contract exists only under UCC § 2-204, by analogy.
oe: Correct. R2d § 22(2) applies to all contracts, not only goods. The parties' year of conduct shows mutual assent.
Section 22(2) isn't limited to goods.
Restitution would be a fallback, but the conduct shows a real contract.
The common law has its own rule in § 22(2).
topic: Wks 2–3 · The offer — Formation by conduct (services)

q: Lou offers to sell Gwen his tractor for $10,000. Gwen replies, “I'll give you $9,000.” Lou says, “No.” Gwen then says, “All right, I accept your offer at $10,000.” Lou has changed his mind and refuses. Is there a contract?
o: No: Gwen's counter-offer ended her power to accept.
Yes: Gwen accepted the exact terms Lou proposed.
Yes: an offer remains open for a reasonable time despite a counter-offer.
No, because a tractor sale over $500 needs a signed writing.
oe: Correct. A counter-offer is an offer on the same matter proposing a substituted bargain, and it terminates the original power of acceptance (R2d § 39). Gwen's “acceptance” is a new offer Lou may reject.
The power to accept those terms ended when Gwen countered.
Lapse is one way an offer ends. A counter-offer is another, and it came first.
The Statute of Frauds isn't the issue. There's no acceptance to enforce.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Counter-offer kills the offer

q: Variation: Same facts, except Gwen's first reply was, “Would you consider taking $9,000?” Lou said, “No, $10,000 is my price.” Gwen then said, “All right, I accept at $10,000.” Is there a contract?
o: Yes: asking whether Lou would take less was a mere inquiry, not a counter.
No: any mention of a different price terminates the offer.
No: Lou's “No” was a revocation of the offer.
Yes, but only if Lou had promised to hold the offer open.
oe: Correct. A mere inquiry, such as “Would you take less?”, doesn't propose a substituted bargain, so the original offer stayed open.
Only a counter-offer or rejection terminates. An inquiry doesn't.
Lou rejected the suggestion and reaffirmed his price. That keeps the offer alive.
No promise is needed. The offer simply hadn't been terminated.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Mere inquiry
pre: Lou offers to sell Gwen his tractor for $10,000. Gwen replies, “I'll give you $9,000.” Lou says, “No.” Gwen then says, “All right, I accept your offer at $10,000.” Lou has changed his mind and refuses. Is there a contract?

q: Variation: Same facts as the original question, except Lou's offer said, “If you want to counter, go ahead — this $10,000 offer stays on the table until Friday regardless.” Gwen countered at $9,000, Lou declined, and on Thursday Gwen accepted at $10,000. Is there a contract?
o: Yes: Lou's offer said a counter-offer wouldn't end Gwen's power to accept.
No: a counter-offer always terminates the power of acceptance.
No: Lou's promise to keep it open was unsupported by consideration.
Yes, but only because the tractor is a good and Lou is a merchant.
oe: Correct. Section 39 makes the counter-offer rule yield to a contrary indication by the offeror.
The rule yields to a contrary statement by the offeror or offeree.
Lou didn't revoke, so revocability doesn't matter. The question is only whether the counter-offer terminated the offer.
The result comes from § 39, not from any merchant rule.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Offeror keeps it open
pre: Lou offers to sell Gwen his tractor for $10,000. Gwen replies, “I'll give you $9,000.” Lou says, “No.” Gwen then says, “All right, I accept your offer at $10,000.” Lou has changed his mind and refuses. Is there a contract?

q: Dev offers to sell Ivy a commercial lot for $300,000, the offer to remain open 30 days. Ivy replies on day 3: “I can't commit at $300,000 right now, but I'm keeping your offer under consideration and will get back to you.” On day 20, Ivy accepts. Dev argues Ivy rejected the offer on day 3. Is there a contract?
o: Yes: taking an offer under advisement isn't a rejection.
No: saying she couldn't commit was a rejection.
No: any response that doesn't accept is a counter-offer.
Yes, because Dev's promise to hold the offer open for 30 days made it irrevocable.
oe: Correct. Section 38: a manifestation of intent not to accept doesn't terminate the power if the offeree says she is taking the offer under further advisement.
Ivy expressly kept the offer under consideration.
A counter-offer proposes a substituted bargain. Ivy proposed nothing.
Without consideration that promise isn't binding, but Dev never revoked, so that isn't the issue.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Further advisement

q: On Monday, Rosa mails Felix a rejection of his offer to sell her his food truck. On Tuesday, she changes her mind and phones Felix: “I accept.” Felix receives the mailed rejection on Wednesday. Is there a contract?
o: Yes: Rosa's acceptance reached Felix before her rejection did.
No: the rejection was effective when mailed on Monday.
No: once an offeree sends a rejection, any later acceptance is a counter-offer.
Yes, because a phone acceptance always beats a mailed rejection.
oe: Correct. A mailed rejection is effective only on receipt (§ 40). An acceptance that arrives before the rejection is effective.
Rejections are effective on receipt, not dispatch.
That's true only if the rejection arrives first.
The medium doesn't matter. What matters is which communication Felix received first.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Rejection then acceptance by mail

q: Variation: Same facts, except Rosa mails her acceptance on Tuesday instead of phoning. The rejection reaches Felix on Wednesday; the acceptance reaches him on Thursday. Is there a contract?
o: No: because the rejection arrived first, Rosa's later acceptance is only a counter-offer.
Yes: the acceptance was effective on dispatch Tuesday under the mailbox rule.
Yes, because the rejection wasn't effective until Wednesday, after the acceptance was mailed.
No, because a rejection is effective on dispatch.
oe: Correct. Under § 40, when the offeree sends a rejection and then an acceptance, the mailbox rule doesn't apply; the acceptance is a counter-offer unless it arrives first.
Section 40 overrides the dispatch rule when a rejection was sent first.
That logic is exactly what § 40 rejects. The acceptance must arrive first to count.
Rejections are effective on receipt. The result follows from § 40's special rule, not dispatch.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Rejection arrives first
pre: On Monday, Rosa mails Felix a rejection of his offer to sell her his food truck. On Tuesday, she changes her mind and phones Felix: “I accept.” Felix receives the mailed rejection on Wednesday. Is there a contract?

q: On a morning when crude oil prices are swinging wildly, a broker emails a refinery an offer to sell 10,000 barrels at $74/barrel. The offer states no deadline. The refinery replies “We accept” three weeks later, after prices have climbed to $90. Is there a contract?
o: No: the offer lapsed after a reasonable time, which was short in this market.
Yes: an offer without a deadline stays open until revoked.
Yes: three weeks is a reasonable time for any written offer.
No, because an emailed offer must be accepted the same day.
oe: Correct. Without a stated time, an offer lapses at the end of a reasonable time, which depends on the deal, market volatility, and the medium (§ 41). A late acceptance is a counter-offer.
Every offer lapses after a reasonable time.
Reasonableness depends on the circumstances; a fast-moving commodity market and an email offer point to a short window.
There's no fixed same-day rule; it's a reasonable time.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Lapse in a volatile market

q: Variation: Same facts, except after receiving the refinery's late “We accept,” the broker replies, “Confirmed — shipping Monday.” Is there a contract?
o: Yes: the broker accepted the refinery's counter-offer.
No: an offer that has lapsed can never form a contract.
Yes: the broker's reply revived the original offer retroactively.
No, because the broker's reply wasn't signed.
oe: Correct. A late acceptance operates as a counter-offer, which the original offeror can accept.
The lapsed offer can't, but the late acceptance is itself a new offer.
Nothing is revived. A new contract forms on the counter-offer.
The question is formation. A signature isn't needed to accept.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Offeror accepts the late acceptance
pre: On a morning when crude oil prices are swinging wildly, a broker emails a refinery an offer to sell 10,000 barrels at $74/barrel. The offer states no deadline. The refinery replies “We accept” three weeks later, after prices have climbed to $90. Is there a contract?

q: On Monday, Hal signs a note offering to sell his lake lot to Kim for $90,000, “this offer open until noon Friday.” Kim pays nothing. On Wednesday, Hal sells the lot to Jay. That evening, Kim's neighbor, a reliable real-estate agent who handled the closing, tells Kim about the sale. On Thursday, Kim hands Hal a written acceptance. Is there a contract between Hal and Kim?
o: No: Kim's power ended when she reliably learned Hal had sold the lot to someone else.
Yes: Hal promised in a signed writing to keep the offer open until Friday.
Yes: revocation is effective only when the offeror himself communicates it.
No, because a sale to a third person terminates the offer whether or not Kim learns of it.
oe: Correct. Dickinson v. Dodds and R2d § 43: the power ends when the offeror takes definite action inconsistent with the offer and the offeree acquires reliable information of it. The promise to hold the offer open was a bare promise without consideration.
Without consideration (or a § 87(1) recital), that promise doesn't make the offer irrevocable.
Revocation can be indirect, learned from a reliable third person.
The offeree must acquire reliable information of the inconsistent act. Without that, the power continues.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Indirect revocation

q: Variation: Same facts, except no one tells Kim about the sale, and she hands Hal her acceptance Thursday morning. What result?
o: There's a contract, and Hal is in breach because he can't deliver the lot.
No contract: the sale to Jay revoked the offer automatically.
No contract: Hal's offer was revocable at any time.
There's a contract, and Jay must give the lot to Kim.
oe: Correct. Without a direct revocation or reliable information reaching Kim, her power of acceptance continued, so her acceptance formed a contract.
Indirect revocation requires the offeree to acquire reliable information.
Revocable, yes, but it must actually be revoked, and it wasn't.
Kim has a contract claim against Hal, not a property claim against Jay.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Offeree never learns
pre: On Monday, Hal signs a note offering to sell his lake lot to Kim for $90,000, “this offer open until noon Friday.” Kim pays nothing. On Wednesday, Hal sells the lot to Jay. That evening, Kim's neighbor, a reliable real-estate agent who handled the closing, tells Kim about the sale. On Thursday, Kim hands Hal a written acceptance. Is there a contract between Hal and Kim?

q: On June 1, a seller mails a buyer an offer. On June 3, the seller mails a revocation. On June 4, the buyer, not yet having received the revocation, mails an acceptance. The revocation reaches the buyer on June 5, and the acceptance reaches the seller on June 6. Is there a contract?
o: Yes: the acceptance was effective on dispatch, June 4, before revocation arrived.
No: the revocation was effective when mailed on June 3.
No: the revocation arrived before the acceptance did.
Yes, formed on June 6 when the seller received the acceptance.
oe: Correct. Acceptance is effective on dispatch (§ 63(a)), but revocation is effective only on receipt (§ 42). The acceptance went out before the revocation arrived.
Revocations are effective on receipt.
Acceptance doesn't wait for arrival. It was effective when mailed.
Under the dispatch rule the contract formed when the acceptance was mailed.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Revocation by mail vs. acceptance by mail

q: On Monday, Abe mails his nephew an offer to sell his fishing cabin for $60,000. Abe dies suddenly on Tuesday. On Wednesday, the nephew, not knowing of the death, mails an acceptance. Abe's estate refuses to convey. Is there a contract?
o: No: Abe's death ended the power of acceptance, even though no one told the nephew.
Yes: the nephew didn't know of the death, so his acceptance was effective.
Yes: the estate stands in Abe's shoes and is bound by his offers.
No, because the acceptance was mailed rather than delivered in person.
oe: Correct. R2d § 48: death or incapacity of the offeror or offeree terminates the power, even though the offeree doesn't know of it.
Notice isn't required for death to terminate the power.
The estate is bound by Abe's contracts, but an unaccepted offer dies with him.
The medium is irrelevant. The power ended before the acceptance.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Death of the offeror

q: Variation: Same facts, except the nephew had paid Abe $1,000 for a 60-day option to buy the cabin for $60,000, and he exercises it on Wednesday. Is the estate bound?
o: Yes: option contracts survive the offeror's death.
No: death terminates every offer, including options.
No, unless the nephew exercised the option before learning of the death.
Yes, but only if the option was recorded.
oe: Correct. Death terminates ordinary offers but not option contracts. The option is already a contract limiting the power to revoke.
The death rule doesn't apply to option contracts.
Knowledge is irrelevant; the option survives either way.
Recording isn't required for the option to bind the estate.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Paid option survives death
pre: On Monday, Abe mails his nephew an offer to sell his fishing cabin for $60,000. Abe dies suddenly on Tuesday. On Wednesday, the nephew, not knowing of the death, mails an acceptance. Abe's estate refuses to convey. Is there a contract?

q: A seller offers to sell a building to Quinn for $1.2 million, stating: “This offer may be accepted only if you deliver a bank's written loan commitment to me by May 1.” Quinn can't get a commitment by May 1. On May 3 he tenders the full price in cash and says he accepts. Is there a contract?
o: No: the power ended when the condition of acceptance failed.
Yes: cash in full is better than a loan commitment, so the condition is excused.
Yes: the offer stayed open for a reasonable time after May 1.
No, because an offer to sell land must be accepted in a signed writing.
oe: Correct. Under R2d § 36(2), the power of acceptance terminates on the non-occurrence of any condition of acceptance under the terms of the offer.
The offeror is master of the offer and set a condition; a substitute performance doesn't satisfy it.
The failure of the condition terminated the power.
The result comes from the failed condition, not a writing requirement.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Condition of acceptance

q: A prosecutor offers a defendant a plea deal of six years. Defense counsel tells the defendant that countering at four years would likely kill the offer, and the defendant declines to counter. The prosecutor withdraws the offer a week later. The defendant then says he'll take six years after all. Later, convicted and sentenced to 15 years, he argues counsel was ineffective for not countering. Applying contract principles, what's the best analysis?
o: A four-year counter would have rejected the six-year offer, and the withdrawn offer couldn't be revived.
The defendant could still accept, because plea offers stay open until trial.
The defendant's acceptance revived the offer because the prosecutor never formally revoked it in writing.
Contract principles don't apply to plea bargaining.
oe: Correct. People v. Robinson: plea bargains are analyzed under contract principles. A counter-offer ends the power of acceptance, and once an offer is withdrawn, a later “acceptance” can't revive it.
Plea offers can be withdrawn like any offer before acceptance.
The withdrawal was the revocation. No writing is required.
Robinson applied contract principles to plea bargains.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Plea offer withdrawn

q: Jade, a homeowner, tells Pete, “I'll sell you my lawn tractor for $400, and I'll keep this offer open for ten days.” Pete gives nothing for the promise. On day 3, Jade calls Pete and says the deal is off. On day 5, Pete says he accepts. Is there a contract?
o: No: Jade's offer was revocable before acceptance.
Yes: Jade promised to keep the offer open for ten days.
Yes: an offer for goods is irrevocable for a reasonable time.
No, because a sale of goods requires a writing.
oe: Correct. Absent consideration or another basis for irrevocability (§§ 25, 45, 87, or § 2-205), an offer can be revoked any time before acceptance.
A bare promise to hold an offer open isn't binding without consideration or another basis.
Only a merchant's signed firm offer is irrevocable without consideration (§ 2-205). This was oral, from a non-merchant.
$400 is under $500, so the Statute of Frauds isn't a problem. The offer was revoked.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Oral promise to hold open

q: A seller offers a buyer 500 tons of scrap steel at $300/ton, adding: “Even if you say no now, you can still accept any time before Friday.” The buyer replies, “No thanks, too high.” On Thursday, the buyer accepts. Is there a contract?
o: Yes: a rejection doesn't terminate the power when the offeror has said otherwise.
No: the buyer's “No thanks” was a rejection that ended the offer.
No: the seller's statement was a promise to keep the offer open without consideration.
Yes, but only because both parties are merchants.
oe: Correct. Under § 38, a rejection terminates the power of acceptance unless the offeror has manifested a contrary intention, as this seller did.
Ordinarily yes, but the offeror expressly kept the power alive.
The seller never revoked. The statement only changed the effect of a rejection.
The result comes from § 38, not merchant status.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Offeror invites reconsideration

q: A prosecutor offers a defendant an eight-year plea, open until the next hearing. Defense counsel asks, “Would the State consider seven?” The prosecutor says, “No, eight is the offer.” The next day, before the hearing and before any withdrawal, the defendant says he accepts the eight-year deal. Applying the contract principles used in People v. Robinson, was the offer still open?
o: Yes: asking about seven years was a mere inquiry.
No: any mention of a lower number rejects a plea offer.
No: plea offers lapse as soon as defense counsel responds.
Yes, because contract principles don't apply to plea bargains.
oe: Correct. Robinson applied contract rules to plea offers. A counter-offer would have ended the offer, but an inquiry (“Would the State consider seven?”) doesn't (§ 61), and the offer hadn't been withdrawn.
Only a counter-offer or rejection terminates the power.
The offer stated it was open until the hearing.
Robinson held they do; that's what keeps the offer open here.
topic: Wk 3 · Termination of the power of acceptance — Plea inquiry, then acceptance

q: Ruth pays Sam $2,000 for a written 90-day option to buy his warehouse for $500,000. On day 30, a developer offers Sam $650,000, and Sam writes Ruth that the option is revoked. On day 60, Ruth gives written notice exercising the option. Is Sam bound to sell to Ruth?
o: Yes: an option supported by consideration limits Sam's power to revoke.
No: Sam revoked before Ruth exercised.
No: the developer's higher offer shows the option price is no longer fair.
Yes, but only if Ruth's notice reached Sam before he signed with the developer.
oe: Correct. An option contract is a promise that meets the requirements for a contract and limits the promisor's power to revoke (R2d § 25). Ruth paid for it.
An option can't be revoked during its term.
Changes in market value don't affect a paid option.
Sam's attempted revocation was ineffective, so the timing of the developer deal doesn't matter.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Irrevocable offers — Paid option

q: Owner signs a writing: “In consideration of $1, receipt of which is acknowledged, I grant Buyer the option to purchase my lot at 12 Elm Street for $80,000 (its appraised value) at any time within 60 days.” Buyer never actually pays the dollar. On day 10, Owner revokes. On day 20, Buyer exercises. Under the Restatement (Second), is Owner bound?
o: Yes: § 87(1)(a) makes the signed, recited offer a binding option.
No: consideration that is recited but never paid is no consideration at all.
No: $1 is too small to support a $80,000 option.
Yes, but only if Buyer relied on the option before Owner revoked.
oe: Correct. Under § 87(1)(a), a false recital of consideration still works if the offer is in a signed writing and proposes an exchange on fair terms within a reasonable time.
That's the minority Burgess view. Section 87(1)(a) treats the recital as enough.
Nominal consideration is fine under § 87(1)(a), which doesn't require payment at all.
Reliance is the § 87(2) route. Section 87(1)(a) needs no reliance.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Irrevocable offers — Recited but unpaid consideration (R2d)

q: Variation: Same facts, but the state follows Board of Control of Eastern Michigan University v. Burgess. Owner proves she told Buyer on day 10 that she was withdrawing. What result?
o: Owner isn't bound: with the dollar unpaid, the “option” was a revocable offer, and she revoked.
Owner is bound, because the writing acknowledged receipt of the dollar.
Owner is bound, because Buyer could have tendered the dollar at any time.
Owner isn't bound, because options for land must be paid in full up front.
oe: Correct. Burgess (substance over form): where nominal consideration is neither paid nor tendered, the option is only a revocable offer. The court remanded on whether Burgess revoked before the notice of exercise; here she did.
Under Burgess, the acknowledgment doesn't substitute for actual payment or tender.
Buyer didn't tender before revocation, and Burgess requires payment or tender.
Only the option consideration matters, and it can be nominal if actually paid.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Irrevocable offers — Burgess view

On day 10, Owner revokes. On day 20, Buyer exercises. Under the Restatement (Second), is Owner bound?

q: A struggling widow signs a writing reciting “$1 in hand paid” and giving a neighbor a ten-year option to buy her family farm at $50,000, a price fixed today. Within two years, nearby development drives the farm's value to $600,000, and the neighbor exercises. The dollar was never paid. Under § 87(1)(a), what's the strongest argument against enforcing the option?
o: The exchange it proposes isn't fair or within a reasonable time.
The writing isn't signed by the neighbor.
Section 87(1)(a) never applies to land.
Options are void if the property's value changes after they're made.
oe: Correct. Section 87(1)(a) requires more than a recital. The writing must propose an exchange on fair terms within a reasonable time. A ten-year fixed-price option for a nominal, unpaid sum is vulnerable on both counts.
Section 87(1)(a) requires the offeror's signature, which the widow gave.
It applies to offers generally, including land.
There's no such rule. The fairness inquiry looks at the terms proposed.

q: Lena tells Rory: “I'll pay you $3,000 to paint my barn by September 1. I don't want your promise — just do the job.” Rory buys paint, then starts scraping and painting the barn's north wall. Halfway through, Lena says, “I've changed my mind. Stop.” Can Lena revoke?
o: No: once Rory began the invited performance, an option contract arose.
Yes: an offer for a unilateral contract can be revoked any time before performance is complete.
No: Rory accepted by beginning, so a bilateral contract binds both parties.
Yes, because Lena expressly said she didn't want a promise.
oe: Correct. Under R2d § 45(1), when an offer invites acceptance only by performance, the offeree's tender or beginning of performance creates an option contract. Lena's duty remains conditional on Rory's completion (§ 45(2)).
That was the old rule. Section 45 protects the offeree who has begun.
Section 45 creates an option, not a bilateral contract. Rory isn't bound to finish.
That's what makes this a performance-only offer to which § 45 applies.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Irrevocable offers — Beginning invited performance

q: Variation: Same facts, except Lena revokes after Rory has bought the paint and rented a ladder, but before he has touched the barn. Does § 45 protect Rory?
o: No: mere preparation isn't beginning performance.
Yes: buying supplies is the first step of performance.
Yes: any expenditure in reliance makes the offer irrevocable under § 45.
No, and Rory has no possible claim of any kind.
oe: Correct. Section 45 cmt. f: preparing to perform isn't beginning the invited performance. Rory might argue reliance under § 87(2) or § 90 for his costs.
Preparation is distinguished from beginning the performance itself.
Section 45 turns on beginning performance. Reliance is the separate § 87(2) route.
Reliance-based claims for his out-of-pocket costs remain possible.

q: Variation: Same facts as the original question, except Lena never tries to revoke. Halfway through, Rory decides the job isn't worth it and walks away. Lena hires someone else for $3,500. Can Lena recover the extra $500 from Rory?
o: No: under § 45, Rory never promised to finish, so walking away isn't a breach.
Yes: beginning performance accepted the offer and bound Rory to finish.
Yes, because § 32 presumes Rory accepted by promise.
No, but Rory can recover half the price for the work done.
oe: Correct. Section 45 binds the offeror (by making the offer irrevocable), not the offeree. Lena's duty to pay is conditional on completion, and she owes Rory nothing for half a barn.
Under § 45 the offeree isn't bound. That's the point of the option analysis.
The § 32 presumption applies only in case of doubt. Lena expressly asked for performance only.
Lena's duty is conditional on complete performance (§ 45(2)).

q: Seller signs an offer to sell her house for $400,000 and promises broker Ty a 6% commission if he produces a buyer at that price within ten days. Ty spends three days advertising, holding an open house, and showing the house to several prospects. On day 4, Seller revokes. On day 7, Ty brings a buyer who signs at $400,000. Is Seller bound to pay the commission?
o: Yes: Ty's beginning made the offer irrevocable for ten days.
No: an offer to pay a broker is revocable until the broker produces a buyer.
No: Seller's duty arose only if she agreed to the buyer's terms.
Yes, but only because the offer promised exclusivity.
oe: Correct. Marchiondo v. Scheck: where an offer invites acceptance by performance, the offeree's beginning of performance creates an option contract (§ 45). Ty finished within the ten days.
That's the trial court's view, which Marchiondo reversed.
The buyer met the offer's terms: $400,000 within ten days.
Marchiondo stressed that the beginning of performance, not exclusivity, makes the offer irrevocable.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Irrevocable offers — Broker's part performance

q: Variation: Same facts, except Ty doesn't find a buyer until day 14. What result?
o: No commission: Ty didn't produce a buyer within ten days.
Commission owed: once Ty began performance, the offer became irrevocable indefinitely.
Commission owed, because Seller's revocation excused the deadline.
Half the commission, for the part performance.
oe: Correct. Under § 45(2), the offeror's duty stays conditional on complete performance per the offer, here within ten days.
The option lasts for the period the offer states.
The revocation was ineffective, so it didn't change the terms.
There's no partial payment rule in § 45; the duty depends on completion.

q: General contractor GC is bidding on a school project. Paving sub PS phones in a bid of $90,000, the lowest. GC uses PS's number in computing its own bid, and the school awards GC the contract. The next day, PS says it made a mistake and won't do the work for less than $140,000. Can GC hold PS to $90,000?
o: Likely yes: GC reasonably relied on PS's bid.
No: GC hadn't accepted PS's bid before PS revoked.
No: an oral bid can't be irrevocable.
Yes, because a subcontractor's bid is a firm offer under § 2-205.
oe: Correct. R2d § 87(2): an offer the offeror should reasonably expect to induce substantial reliance before acceptance, and which does, is binding as an option to the extent necessary to avoid injustice. ◆ This is Drennan v. Star Paving.
Section 87(2) protects reliance before acceptance.
Section 87(2) doesn't require a writing.
Paving is a service, and the bid wasn't a signed writing. The basis is reliance.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Irrevocable offers — Subcontractor's bid

q: Variation: Same facts, except GC computed its bid using another paver's $95,000 number and only received PS's lower bid after submitting. What result?
o: PS may withdraw: GC didn't rely on PS's bid in computing its own bid.
GC can still hold PS to $90,000 because PS's bid was the lowest.
PS is bound because GC planned to use its bid on future jobs.
PS is bound because subcontractor bids are irrevocable by custom.
oe: Correct. Section 87(2) requires that the offer actually induce the reliance. GC's bid wasn't based on PS's number.
Being lowest doesn't create an option without reliance or consideration.
Speculative future reliance isn't enough.
No such general rule exists.
