q: An office-supply wholesaler sends a law firm a signed letter: “We offer 500 ergonomic chairs at $210 each. This price is guaranteed for 30 days.” The law firm pays nothing for the promise. On day 10, the wholesaler writes that it is withdrawing the offer. On day 20, the firm accepts. Is there a contract?
o: Yes: a merchant's signed written assurance is a firm offer under § 2-205.
No: the firm gave no consideration to keep the offer open.
No: § 2-205 applies only if both parties are merchants.
Yes, but only for a reasonable time, which ended before day 20.
oe: Correct. UCC § 2-205: a merchant's signed written offer to buy or sell goods that by its terms gives assurance it will be held open is irrevocable for the stated time, up to three months. It's the leading example of an offer made irrevocable by statute (R2d § 87(1)(b)).
Section 2-205 dispenses with consideration.
Only the offeror must be a merchant.
The offer states 30 days, so that's the period.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Irrevocable offers — Merchant firm offer

q: Variation: Same facts, except the letter guarantees the price “for six months.” The wholesaler revokes in month 4, and the firm accepts in month 5. Is there a contract?
o: No: the firm-offer period maxes out at three months, so it was revocable by month 4.
Yes: the wholesaler promised six months in a signed writing.
No: an offer that promises more than three months is void from the start.
Yes: an offer for a stated time can't be revoked until that time runs.
oe: Correct. The § 2-205 period may not exceed three months. The offer doesn't die then; it becomes an ordinary revocable offer, and the wholesaler revoked it.
The statute caps irrevocability without consideration at three months.
It's irrevocable for the first three months, then revocable.
That's only true for options and firm offers within the cap.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Irrevocable offers — More than three months
pre: An office-supply wholesaler sends a law firm a signed letter: “We offer 500 ergonomic chairs at $210 each. This price is guaranteed for 30 days.” The law firm pays nothing for the promise. On day 10, the wholesaler writes that it is withdrawing the offer. On day 20, the firm accepts. Is there a contract?

q: Variation: Same facts as the six-month variation, except the law firm paid the wholesaler $500 for the six-month guarantee. What result?
o: Yes: with consideration paid, it's a common-law option for the full six months.
No contract: § 2-205 caps all firm offers at three months.
No contract: the $500 converts the deal into a services contract.
There's a contract only if the firm accepted within the first three months.
oe: Correct. The three-month cap applies to firm offers without consideration. A paid option binds for its stated term (§ 25).
The cap doesn't limit an option supported by consideration.
Paying for an option doesn't change the subject matter.
With consideration, the whole six months is protected.

q: A buyer sends a seller its own pre-printed request-for-quote form. In fine print in the middle, the form says: “Seller agrees the prices quoted will be held firm for 60 days.” The seller fills in prices and signs once at the bottom, where the form says “Seller's signature.” On day 15, the seller revokes. Is the seller bound for 60 days?
o: No: the offeror didn't separately sign the term.
Yes: the seller signed the form, which contained a written assurance.
Yes: firm-offer terms are binding whenever both parties are merchants.
No, because 60 days exceeds the firm-offer cap.
oe: Correct. Section 2-205 requires a separate signature by the offeror when the firm-offer term is on the offeree's form, to prevent a merchant from unknowingly binding itself.
A single signature at the bottom isn't the separate signing § 2-205 demands for the offeree's form.
Merchant status doesn't cure the missing separate signature.
The cap is three months, so 60 days is fine. The defect is the signature.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Irrevocable offers — Assurance on the offeree's form

q: A building-materials supplier's sales manager tells a contractor over the phone: “I'll hold this lumber price for you for 30 days, guaranteed.” Nothing is put in writing. On day 5, the supplier raises its prices and revokes. Is the supplier bound?
o: No: a firm offer must be in a signed writing, so the oral assurance was revocable.
Yes: the supplier is a merchant, and merchant assurances are binding.
Yes: the word “guaranteed” supplies the consideration.
No, because firm offers apply only to sellers who manufacture goods.
oe: Correct. Section 2-205 requires a signed writing. An oral assurance, without consideration, leaves the offer revocable.
Merchant status is necessary but not sufficient; the writing requirement isn't met.
Words of assurance aren't consideration.
Any merchant offering to buy or sell goods can make a firm offer.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Irrevocable offers — Oral firm offer

q: Gail's signed offer to sell her antique desk says: “Acceptance must be made only by a signed letter delivered to my office.” Hugo, the offeree, emails Gail a clear “I accept your offer” the next day. Gail, having found a better buyer, ignores it. Is there a contract?
o: No: Gail required a particular manner of acceptance, and Hugo didn't use it.
Yes: any reasonable medium is acceptable.
Yes: email is faster than a letter, so it's a superior medium.
No, because email acceptances are never effective for goods.
oe: Correct. The offeror is master of the offer and may require acceptance in a particular manner (R2d § 50(1)). Acceptance must be made in the manner the offer requires.
That's the default rule (§ 30), which applies only unless the offer indicates otherwise.
When the offer requires a manner, a “better” manner doesn't substitute.
Email can be a reasonable medium. The problem here is the offer's express requirement.
topic: Wk 4 · Acceptance: manner, timing & silence — Required manner of acceptance

q: Variation: Same facts, except Gail's offer says, “You can reply by letter to my office.” Hugo promptly emails, “I accept.” Is there a contract?
o: Yes: the offer suggested letters but didn't require one.
No: the offer specified a letter, so only a letter can accept.
No: an acceptance must use the same medium as the offer.
Yes, but only after the email is printed and signed.
oe: Correct. Unless otherwise indicated, an offer invites acceptance in any manner and by any medium reasonable in the circumstances (§ 30; § 2-206(1)(a)).
“You can” suggests; it doesn't require.
There's no same-medium requirement; reasonableness controls.
No signature or printout is needed to accept.

q: Uncle Ray, who is ill, writes his niece Tess and her husband: “If you'll move here and help run my nursery and care for me, you'll inherit the nursery when I die.” They write back, “We accept and will come next month.” Before they arrive, Ray dies; his will leaves the nursery to a charity. Tess and her husband sue. What result?
o: They win: a bilateral contract formed when they promised, before Ray died.
They lose: the offer sought performance, which they never began before Ray died.
They lose: Ray's death terminated the offer.
They win, but only restitution for their travel costs.
oe: Correct. Davis v. Jacoby: in case of doubt, an offer is presumed to invite acceptance by promise or performance (§ 32), so their promissory letter accepted. Death doesn't terminate an offer already accepted.
The offer was ambiguous, and in case of doubt the offeree may accept by promise.
Death ends an unaccepted offer. This one had already been accepted.
In Davis, the offerees performed afterward and got specific performance.
topic: Wk 4 · Acceptance: manner, timing & silence — Doubt: promise or performance?

q: Variation: Same facts, except Ray's letter says: “Don't write back. A letter means nothing to me — only your arrival here will count as your answer.” Tess and her husband write back promising to come, but Ray dies before they leave. What result?
o: They lose: the offer required performance, which never began.
They win: under Davis v. Jacoby, an offeree may always accept by promise.
They win: their letter began performance.
They win restitution of the full value of the nursery.
oe: Correct. The § 32 presumption applies only in case of doubt. Here the offeror, as master of the offer, required performance, so the promissory letter didn't accept, and death terminated the unaccepted offer (§ 48).
Only when it's unclear what the offer invites.
Writing back isn't the invited performance (arriving and caring for Ray).
There's no contract and no benefit conferred to restore.

Tess and her husband sue. What result?

q: VitaShield advertises: “We will pay $500 to anyone who catches the flu after taking VitaShield daily for 30 days as directed. We've deposited $50,000 with First Bank to show our sincerity.” Mae buys VitaShield, takes it as directed for 30 days, and then catches the flu. She never told VitaShield she was taking it. VitaShield refuses to pay, calling the ad puffery and noting she never notified it of acceptance. What result?
o: Mae recovers: she accepted by performing.
VitaShield wins: ads are invitations to deal, never offers.
VitaShield wins: Mae had to notify it before she started taking the product.
VitaShield wins: Mae gave no consideration.
oe: Correct. Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball: an ad seeking a performance can be an offer, and the bank deposit showed seriousness. When the offer seeks performance, notice isn't required unless requested (§ 54(1)).
An ad that is specific and seeks a performance, like a reward, can be an offer.
The nature of the offer dispensed with notice.
Using the product as directed, at VitaShield's request, is consideration.
topic: Wk 4 · Acceptance: manner, timing & silence — Reward ad and notice

q: Variation: Same facts, except the ad adds: “To qualify, register with us by email before starting your 30-day course.” Mae never registers. Can she recover?
o: No: when the offer itself requests notice, performance alone isn't enough.
Yes: in a unilateral contract, notice is never required.
Yes: VitaShield's bank deposit waived any notice requirement.
No, because ads can never be offers.
oe: Correct. Under § 54(1), notice of acceptance by performance isn't needed unless the offer requests it. VitaShield made registration part of the terms.
The no-notice default yields when the offer requests notice.
The deposit showed seriousness; it didn't waive the offer's own terms.
The ad was an offer; she just didn't meet its terms.
topic: Wk 4 · Acceptance: manner, timing & silence — Offer requests notice

q: Nell, who lives in Chicago, writes to a lumber yard in rural Alaska: “If you extend up to $20,000 in credit to my nephew for his cabin, I'll guarantee payment.” The yard extends $20,000 in credit but never tells Nell. Eleven months later the nephew defaults, and the yard writes Nell for the first time demanding payment. Nell had no other way of learning of the credit. Is Nell liable?
o: Probably not: the yard never used diligence to tell her.
Yes: an offer accepted by performance never requires notice.
Yes: the yard's performance formed a contract the moment the credit was extended.
No: guaranty offers must always be accepted by a return promise.
oe: Correct. Under § 54(2), when the offeree has reason to know the offeror won't learn of the performance with reasonable promptness, the offeror's duty is discharged unless the offeree uses reasonable diligence to notify, the offeror learns within a reasonable time, or the offer dispenses with notice.
That's the general rule (§ 54(1)), but § 54(2) adds a notice condition in this situation.
The contract formed, but Nell's duty is discharged under § 54(2).
A guaranty offer can invite acceptance by performance, as this one did.
topic: Wk 4 · Acceptance: manner, timing & silence — Acceptance by performance the offeror won't learn of

q: A landlord mails a prospective tenant a signed lease offer, asking her to sign and return it if she agrees. She signs it and puts it in her desk drawer, intending to mail it later, but never does. Two weeks later the landlord leases to someone else. Is there a contract?
o: No: her acceptance was never sent to the landlord.
Yes: signing was the act of acceptance.
Yes: under the mailbox rule, acceptance is effective when made.
No, because a lease offer can be accepted only in person.
oe: Correct. Under § 56, an offeree accepting by promise must use reasonable diligence to notify the offeror, or the acceptance must be received seasonably. A signed form in a drawer does neither.
Uncommunicated assent isn't an effective acceptance by promise.
The dispatch rule requires putting the acceptance out of the offeree's possession.
Nothing requires in-person acceptance. The problem is that it was never sent.

q: A retailer sends a supplier a purchase order: “Ship promptly 300 blue rain jackets, size M, at $40 each.” The supplier, without comment, ships 300 green jackets. The retailer wants to hold the supplier liable. What's the legal effect of the shipment?
o: It's both an acceptance and a breach.
It's a counter-offer that the retailer may accept or reject.
It's neither, because non-conforming goods can't accept an offer.
It's an acceptance, but not a breach, because the seller substantially complied.
oe: Correct. Under UCC § 2-206(1)(b), an order for prompt shipment invites acceptance by prompt shipment of conforming or non-conforming goods. Shipping non-conforming goods without a seasonable notice of accommodation accepts and breaches at once.
That's the result only if the seller notifies the buyer the shipment is an accommodation.
Section 2-206(1)(b) expressly says non-conforming shipment can accept.
Green jackets don't conform to an order for blue; the shipment breaches.
topic: Wk 4 · Acceptance: manner, timing & silence — Shipping non-conforming goods

q: Variation: Same facts, except the supplier includes a note: “We're out of blue. We're sending green as an accommodation, in case they help you.” What's the effect?
o: No acceptance: it's a counter-offer the retailer may reject.
Acceptance and breach, because the supplier shipped the wrong color.
Acceptance of the order for blue, with the supplier obligated to ship blue later.
A breach of the retailer's firm offer.
oe: Correct. A seasonable notice that the shipment is only an accommodation keeps it from being an acceptance, so there's no breach.
The accommodation notice changes the result.
An accommodation isn't an acceptance.
The retailer's order wasn't a firm offer, and an accommodation isn't a breach.

No contract: the rejection arrived first, so it controls.

q: Wade writes to Faye: “I'll sell you my used kayak for $600. If I don't hear from you by Friday, I'll consider it sold.” Faye doesn't want the kayak and ignores the letter. On Saturday, Wade delivers the kayak and demands $600. Is there a contract?

Yes: Faye had a duty to reject in writing.

No: silence is never acceptance between merchants.

q: During settlement talks in a suit a lawyer is handling, the client wires, “Must know immediately your fee if we settle.” The lawyer wires back, “$40,000.” The client says nothing, settles, and directs the lawyer to dismiss the case. After the lawyer does so, the client calls the fee unreasonable and refuses to pay more than $15,000. What result?

The client owes nothing, because a fee agreement must be in writing.

oe: Correct. Laredo National Bank v. Gordon: having asked for the figure, received it, stayed silent, and directed the work to proceed, the client accepted. One who keeps silent, knowing silence will be misinterpreted, can't deny the natural meaning of his conduct.
The client's silence and conduct were an acceptance of the stated fee.
No writing requirement applied, and the conduct formed a contract.
The acceptance came from silence and conduct, not a retainer.

o: No: the client rejected the figure, but it still owes a reasonable fee for the requested work.
Yes: directing the dismissal accepted the $40,000 fee.
No, and the lawyer recovers nothing, because there was no agreed fee.
Yes: once a lawyer names a fee, the client must object in writing within ten days.

No: silence is never acceptance.
No: unordered merchandise is always a gift.
Yes, but only for the reasonable value of the books, not $450.

Exercising dominion is conduct, not mere silence.
Unordered-merchandise statutes typically protect consumers; this is a law firm, and the general rule is § 69(2).
Dominion binds the offeree to the offered terms unless they're manifestly unreasonable.

She owes $450 under § 69(2) because she used the books.
She must return the books or pay their reasonable value.

The statute lets her keep them as a gift.

q: Homeowners sign a remodeler's form for a $30,000 kitchen job. The form says it becomes binding “upon written acceptance by Remodeler or upon commencement of the work.” The remodeler runs credit checks for five days, then loads cabinets onto trucks and drives a crew to the house, only to find another contractor already working. The homeowners had hired the other contractor three days earlier but never told the remodeler. Is there a contract?
o: Yes: the remodeler accepted by commencing work before any revocation reached it.
No: the homeowners revoked by hiring another contractor.
No: loading trucks is only preparation, not performance.
No, because the remodeler took more than a reasonable time to accept.
oe: Correct. Ever-Tite Roofing v. Green: loading trucks and traveling to the site was commencing performance, done within a reasonable time and before notice of revocation. The homeowners' refusal is a breach.
Hiring someone else without telling the remodeler wasn't a communicated revocation.

A few days for credit checks was within a reasonable time.

Yes: the form gave the remodeler the right to accept by commencing work at any time.
Yes: the remodeler's credit check began performance.
No, because home-improvement contracts must be signed by both parties.

Credit checks are the remodeler's own review, not commencement of the work.

The company then mails a letter saying the contract was “approved and processed” and records a lien. No work has begun. Is there a contract?
o: No: the signed form was only an offer, and it was revoked before acceptance.
Yes: the homeowner signed a form that said it was binding.
Yes: the company had an implied reasonable time to accept, during which the offer couldn't be revoked.
Yes: recording the lien was acceptance.
oe: Correct. Loeb v. Johnson: because the company reserved the right to reject for any reason, the homeowner's form was a revocable offer. The cancellation came before any acceptance.

Yes: her post was an objective manifestation of assent.
Yes: the landlord's silence after the post was acceptance.
Yes, under the mailbox rule, as soon as she posted.

A manifestation the offeror can't see isn't communicated to him.

Yes: under § 2-207, an acceptance with additional terms still forms a contract.
Yes: closing costs are a minor term that doesn't affect acceptance.

q: Variation: Same facts, except the acknowledgment says only: “This acceptance is subject to the terms and conditions on the reverse side.” Did the seller make its acceptance expressly conditional?
o: Likely not: the language isn't clear enough.
Yes: any reference to the seller's own terms makes the acceptance conditional.
Yes: “subject to” is the same as “expressly conditional on.”
No, but the reply is a counter-offer anyway because it adds terms.

The seller's acknowledgment says: “Seller's acceptance is expressly conditional on Buyer's assent to the additional and different terms on the reverse side.” The terms include a limitation of remedies. o: No contract: a reply that changes the price isn't an expression of acceptance.
A contract at $700, because the different price term is knocked out.
A contract at $760, because the seller's form had the last word.
A contract at a reasonable price under § 2-305.

The seller's reply is a counter-offer the buyer never accepted.
The open-price gap-filler applies only if the parties intended to contract.

q: Variation: Same facts, except the seller's acknowledgment says: “We accept your order for 600 laptops at $700 each.” The buyer ordered 1,000. Is the acknowledgment an acceptance under § 2-207(1)?

Yes: a contract forms for 600, with the remaining 400 as a proposal.
Yes: a contract forms for 1,000, and the 600 term is knocked out.
Yes, because both parties are merchants.

The knock-out rule applies only once a contract is formed.

The disclaimer controls: the buyer accepted it by continuing to order.
The disclaimer controls through course of dealing.

No: § 2-207(3) always governs when a form is expressly conditional.
No: warranty disclaimers can never be agreed to in a form.

Yes, on the buyer's meaning, because the buyer drafted the term.
Yes, on a reasonable compromise between the two locations.

No contract: the parties meant different things.
A contract on the dealer's meaning, because the dealer performed first.

That's true only if neither or both knew. Here only the dealer did.
Performance doesn't decide meaning. Knowledge does.
Ambiguity known to only one party is resolved against that party.

A contract on the buyer's meaning, because the buyer is paying.

A shared error about a fact doesn't negate assent.

q: A Canadian seller emails a U.S. buyer offering 50 used pallets of tile “for $10,000.” The seller means Canadian dollars. The buyer, a U.S. firm that has dealt with the seller only in U.S. dollars, understands U.S. dollars. The seller knew the buyer had always paid in U.S. dollars, but the buyer had no reason to know the seller meant Canadian dollars this time. The buyer accepts. Which currency governs?

Canadian dollars, because the seller made the offer.
No contract, because the parties attached different meanings.
The average of the two currencies.
oe: Correct. Under § 20(2), the contract is formed on the meaning of the party who didn't know or have reason to know of the other's different meaning.
The offeror's undisclosed meaning doesn't control when the offeree's meaning is reasonable and the offeror had reason to know it.
That's the result only if neither or both had reason to know.
Courts don't split the difference.

q: A contract calls for delivery of “the Steinway in the Hamilton Hall lobby.” The seller's college has two buildings named Hamilton Hall, each with a Steinway in its lobby. The buyer offers testimony showing this. The seller objects that the written contract is clear on its face and outside evidence is inadmissible. How should the court rule?
o: Admit the evidence: it can show a latent ambiguity that may mean there was no agreement.
Exclude it: a writing that is clear on its face can't be contradicted.
Exclude it: the court will enforce the seller's meaning because the seller drafted the contract.
Admit it, but only to reform the contract to the more valuable piano.
oe: Correct. In Raffles v. Wichelhaus, parol evidence showed there were two ships named Peerless. A latent ambiguity appears only from outside facts, which may be proved; if each party meant a different piano and neither knew, there's no contract (§ 20).

Neither party's meaning prevails when neither knew of the other's.
The doctrine asks whether there was assent, not which piano is worth more.

q: At a county fair, a rancher tells a restaurant owner, “I'll sell you some of my best beef cattle at a good price this fall.” The owner says, “Deal.” In the fall, the rancher sells all his cattle elsewhere. The owner sues. What's the rancher's best defense?
o: The terms are too indefinite to enforce.
The price term is missing, and price can never be supplied by a court.
Oral agreements for cattle are never enforceable.
The rancher was only joking.
oe: Correct. Under R2d § 33(2) and UCC § 2-204(3), terms must give a reasonably certain basis for a remedy. There's no quantity gap-filler, and “some” at “a good price” gives a court nothing to enforce.
The UCC can supply a reasonable price (§ 2-305). The fatal gap is quantity.
Indefiniteness is the stronger defense; the Statute of Frauds might also apply, but the agreement fails at formation first.
Nothing suggests a jest. The problem is the lack of definite terms.

The center stops shipping, claiming the contract failed for indefiniteness. What result?
o: The contract stands, with a reasonable price at the time for delivery.
The contract fails, because an agreement to agree on price is unenforceable.
The contract fails for the third quarter only, and the parties may walk away.
The center may set any price it chooses.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-305(1)(b), if price is left to be agreed and the parties fail to agree, the price is a reasonable price at the time for delivery. Section 2-204(3) prevents failure for indefiniteness where the parties intended to contract.

Only a price to be fixed by one party is set by that party, and then in good faith.

q: Variation: Same facts, except the contract says: “If the parties do not agree on a quarterly price, there shall be no obligation for that quarter.” What result for the third quarter?
o: No obligation for that quarter, because the parties said so in advance.
A reasonable price applies anyway under § 2-305(1).
The whole year's contract is void.
The center must ship at the last agreed price.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-305(4), if the parties intend not to be bound unless the price is fixed or agreed, and it isn't, there's no contract (for that portion).
The gap-filler yields to the parties' expressed intent not to be bound.
The clause addresses only the quarter without an agreed price.
Nothing in the contract carries the old price forward.

Yes: the buyer agreed to let the seller set the price.
No: one party can never be given the power to set the price.

That agreement carries an obligation of good faith.

The last published index price.
There's no contract for later deliveries.
Whatever price the seller reasonably chooses.

Freezing the price isn't the statutory answer.

q: A bakery chain agrees to buy “all the flour our stores require” for two years from a mill at a fixed price per pound. The mill later argues there's no contract because no quantity was stated. What result?
o: A contract: the bakery's good-faith requirements set the quantity.
No contract: quantity is essential and can't be left open.
No contract: the bakery could choose to require nothing, so its promise is illusory.
There's a contract, but the mill may set the quantity.

A requirements term states a quantity by reference to an objective measure.
Good faith limits the bakery's discretion.
The bakery's actual requirements set the quantity.

q: A ten-year commercial lease at $2,000 a month gives the tenant an option to renew for ten more years “at a rental to be agreed upon in light of comparative business conditions at the time.” When the tenant exercises the option, the parties can't agree on rent, and the tenant asks the court to set it. o: The clause is unenforceable as an agreement to agree.
The court sets a reasonable rent.
The old rent of $2,000 carries forward.
The landlord may set any rent, and the tenant must take it or leave.

The clause gives neither side that power.

The renewal is enforceable at the land's fair market value for industrial use.
The renewal is unenforceable as an agreement to agree.

An enforceable contract, with a court supplying reasonable terms for each gap.

The duty is limited to the letter's stated period.
The letter wasn't binding as to the sale.

The contract fails: delivery terms are essential.

The buyer loses because the seller said nothing.
The buyer wins damages for deceit automatically.

Weintraub reversed summary judgment despite a similar clause.
Under the modern rule, nondisclosure of a known latent defect can count.
The question is rescission, and the seller's knowledge must still be proved.

She says nothing, makes no statements about pests, doesn't conceal anything, and has no special relationship with the buyer. After closing, the buyer discovers the termites and sues for damages. Under Swinton v. Whitinsville Savings Bank, what result?

q: Buyers inspect a house only in the daytime with all lights on. Before closing, they enter the vacant house at night and find roaches “running in all directions.” The seller, who lived there for years, never mentioned them. The contract says the buyers are “fully satisfied” with the house's condition. The buyers rescind, and the seller sues for the deposit. What must the buyers show to win under Weintraub?
o: The seller knew of the infestation and hid it.
Nothing more: any defect found before closing lets a buyer rescind.
That the seller made an express statement denying the roaches.
That the “fully satisfied” clause was unconscionable.
oe: Correct. Weintraub remanded to determine whether the seller knew of and concealed the infestation. A known, material, latent defect supports rescission despite the clause.
The seller's knowledge and the defect's materiality and latency matter.
Weintraub covers nondisclosure, not only affirmative statements.
The fraud theory doesn't depend on unconscionability.

q: Before listing her house, a seller paints over water stains on the basement ceiling to keep buyers from noticing a leak. She never says anything about water. A buyer, who would have walked away had he known of the leak, signs a contract. Is there a misrepresentation?
o: Yes: hiding the stains asserts there's no leak.
No: the seller said nothing about water.
No: sellers have no duty to disclose defects.
Yes, but only if the buyer asked about leaks.
oe: Correct. Under § 160, action intended to prevent another from learning a fact is equivalent to an assertion that the fact doesn't exist.
Concealment counts as an assertion even without words.
This isn't mere nondisclosure; it's active concealment.
Concealment is an assertion regardless of questions.

q: Variation: Same facts, except the buyer's own inspector found the painted-over stains and told the buyer about the leak before the buyer signed. Can the buyer rescind?
o: No: the buyer didn't rely on the concealment.
Yes: concealment always makes a contract voidable.
Yes, because the seller acted in bad faith.
No, because concealment isn't a misrepresentation.
oe: Correct. Concealment is an assertion (§ 160), but rescission also requires justified reliance (§ 164). The buyer learned of the leak before signing.
Reliance is still required.
Bad faith doesn't replace the reliance element.
It is an assertion under § 160; the claim fails for lack of reliance.

q: Asked about the roof, a seller says, “It was replaced in 2018.” That's true, but the seller doesn't mention that it has leaked badly every spring since. Is there an actionable misrepresentation?
o: Yes: the half-truth is a misrepresentation.
No: the statement was literally true.
No: the buyer should have asked whether the roof leaks.
Yes, but only if the seller wrote the statement down.
oe: Correct. Under § 161(a), non-disclosure equals an assertion when disclosure is necessary to prevent a previous assertion from being a misrepresentation. A misleading half-truth is an assertion not in accord with the facts (§ 159).
Literal truth doesn't save a misleading half-truth.
The seller's statement implied a sound roof.
Oral assertions count.

q: A buyer and a seller agree orally that a used truck will come with new tires. The seller then hands the buyer a written contract that omits the tire term. The seller knows the buyer thinks the tires are included and is signing without reading closely. The seller says nothing. Is the seller's silence a misrepresentation?
o: Yes: the seller's silence about the writing is an assertion.
No: the buyer had a duty to read before signing.
No: silence is never a misrepresentation.
Yes, but only if the seller drafted the writing deceptively.
oe: Correct. That's § 161(c).
Section 161(c) addresses exactly this situation.
Section 161 lists four situations where it is.
Knowing silence about the writing's contents is enough.

q: A trustee buys a parcel of land from the trust's beneficiary. The trustee knows, from trust business, that a highway interchange will be built nearby, sharply raising the land's value, and doesn't tell the beneficiary. Is the nondisclosure a misrepresentation?
o: Yes: the trust relationship required disclosure.
No: parties dealing at arm's length have no duty to disclose.
No: future developments are opinions, not facts.
Yes, but only if the trustee made an express statement about value.
oe: Correct. That's § 161(d).
A trustee and beneficiary aren't at arm's length.
The planned interchange is a present fact known to the trustee.
Silence is enough given the relationship.
topic: Wk 9 · Misrepresentation & nondisclosure — Relationship of trust

q: Variation: Same facts, except the buyer is a stranger to the seller who learned of the planned interchange by reading public planning-commission minutes. The buyer says nothing about it and buys the land. Does § 161(d) require disclosure?
o: No: there's no relation of trust and confidence between them.
Yes: anyone with superior knowledge of value must disclose it.
Yes: the seller is entitled to know because the buyer profited.
No, because public information can never be a misrepresentation.
oe: Correct. Section 161(d) requires disclosure only where the other person is entitled to know because of a relationship of trust and confidence. Strangers at arm's length aren't in one.
No general duty exists to share knowledge of value with a stranger.
Profit doesn't create a relationship of trust.
The point is the absence of a duty to disclose here, not a categorical rule about public information.

q: A seller of a rural property tells a buyer, “I'm certain the well has never run dry,” though the seller has owned the property only three months, has never checked the well records, and has no idea whether it has run dry. In fact it runs dry most summers. Is the misrepresentation fraudulent?
o: Yes: the seller claimed certainty without any basis.
No: the seller didn't know the statement was false.
No: statements about wells are opinions.
Yes, but only if the buyer was harmed.
oe: Correct. Under § 162(1)(b)–(c), an assertion is fraudulent if the maker lacks the confidence he states or implies, or knows he doesn't have the basis he states or implies.
Knowledge of falsity is only one of three routes to fraud.
“Has never run dry” is a statement of fact.
For rescission, the question is fraud or materiality plus justified reliance.
topic: Wk 9 · Misrepresentation & nondisclosure — Confidence without basis

q: A seller tells a buyer that a 1965 convertible was once owned by a famous jazz musician. The seller knows that the buyer, a jazz fanatic, cares deeply about this, though most buyers wouldn't. The claim is false, and the seller knows it. The car is otherwise exactly as described. Can the buyer rescind?
o: Yes: it was fraudulent, and material to this particular buyer.
No: the claim wouldn't matter to a reasonable buyer.
No: the car itself is exactly as described.
Yes, but only if the car is worth less without the history.
oe: Correct. Under § 164, either fraud or materiality suffices. Section 162(2) makes an assertion material if the maker knows it would likely induce this recipient to assent.
Materiality also covers what the maker knows would induce the particular recipient, and fraud alone is enough.
The misrepresentation went to something the buyer valued.
Rescission doesn't require a loss in value.
topic: Wk 9 · Misrepresentation & nondisclosure — Materiality to this recipient

q: An elderly man who can't read English is handed a document by his nephew, who tells him it's a receipt for groceries. It's actually a deed transferring his house to the nephew. He signs. Is the deed void or voidable?
o: Void: this is fraud in the factum.
Voidable, because he was fraudulently induced.
Valid, because he signed it.
Voidable only if the nephew knew the statement was false.
oe: Correct. Fraud in the factum (§ 163): the signer didn't assent to a deed at all, so there's no contract.
Fraud in the inducement makes a contract voidable. Here he didn't know what he was signing.
A signature on a document misdescribed to someone who couldn't know its nature isn't assent.
The doctrine turns on the signer's lack of opportunity to know, and the nephew clearly knew.
topic: Wk 9 · Misrepresentation & nondisclosure — Fraud in the factum

q: Variation: Same facts, except the signer reads English well, had the document in hand for ten minutes, and simply didn't bother to read it. What result?
o: Not fraud in the factum: he could have read it.
Still void, because the nephew lied about the document.
Valid in all events, because he signed.
Void, because family members can't contract with each other.
oe: Correct. Section 163 applies only where the signer neither knows nor has a reasonable opportunity to know. At most, the deed is voidable for fraud in the inducement if his reliance was justified.
The lie matters, but § 163 requires lack of reasonable opportunity to know.
He may still argue fraudulent inducement.
There's no such rule.

q: A seller falsely tells a buyer that a warehouse's roof is new. Before signing, the buyer hires a roofer who inspects and reports the roof is 25 years old and failing. The buyer signs anyway, at the agreed price, then seeks rescission. What result?
o: No rescission: the buyer knew the truth, so he didn't rely on the statement.
Rescission, because the seller's statement was fraudulent.
Rescission, because the roof was material.
Damages for deceit, since rescission is unavailable.
oe: Correct. Section 164 requires that the recipient be justified in relying. The buyer knew the truth from his own inspection.
Fraud alone isn't enough; justified reliance is also required.
Materiality without reliance doesn't support rescission.
Deceit also requires justifiable reliance.
topic: Wk 9 · Misrepresentation & nondisclosure — Justified reliance

q: In March, a seller truthfully tells a prospective buyer, “The basement has never flooded.” In April, while they're still negotiating, a storm floods the basement. The seller repairs the damage cosmetically and says nothing. In May, the buyer signs the purchase contract. He discovers the truth before closing and seeks rescission. What's the best analysis?
o: The seller's silence after the flood counts as an assertion that it never flooded.
No misrepresentation: the statement was true when made.
No misrepresentation: a seller has no duty to update statements made during negotiations.
Rescission is unavailable because the buyer could have inspected again.
oe: Correct. Under § 161(a), nondisclosure equals an assertion when disclosure is needed to prevent a previous assertion from being a misrepresentation. If material and relied on, the contract is voidable (§ 164).
A statement can become a misrepresentation if the speaker learns before the deal is made that it's no longer true and stays silent.
Section 161(a) imposes a duty to correct earlier assertions that have become untrue before the contract is made.
The cosmetic repair makes the reliance more justified, not less.
topic: Wk 9 · Misrepresentation & nondisclosure — Statement that becomes false

q: On March 1, a lumber wholesaler sends a contractor a signed letter: “We offer 50,000 board feet of fir at $900 per thousand, firm until April 1.” The contractor pays nothing for the promise. On March 10, after its costs rise, the wholesaler emails that the offer is withdrawn. On March 15, the contractor replies: “We accept your March 1 offer. If possible, please deliver by rail.” The wholesaler refuses to ship. Is there a contract?
o: Yes: the firm offer couldn't be revoked before April 1, and a request that doesn't condition acceptance is still an acceptance.
No: the wholesaler revoked on March 10, before the contractor accepted.
No: the rail request made the reply a counter-offer.
Yes, but only if the contractor paid something to keep the offer open.
oe: Correct. A merchant's signed firm offer is irrevocable for the stated time without consideration (§ 2-205), so the March 10 withdrawal was ineffective. “If possible, please deliver by rail” is a request, not a condition (§ 61; § 2-207(1)).
Revocation is ineffective during a firm offer's stated period (up to three months).
A request that doesn't condition the acceptance doesn't turn it into a counter-offer.
Section 2-205 dispenses with consideration.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Firm offer, revocation, and a request

q: A machine-tool maker sends a factory a signed price list headed “Quotation — subject to our acceptance of your order.” The factory sends a purchase order that includes a clause requiring disputes to be litigated in its home state. The maker ships with an invoice containing an arbitration clause. Both are merchants. Neither form is expressly conditional. A dispute arises. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The factory's order was the offer, and the dispute clauses conflict.
The quotation was the offer, so the maker's arbitration clause controls.
The invoice was a counter-offer, accepted when the factory took delivery.
The arbitration clause becomes part of the contract because both parties are merchants.
oe: Correct. The quotation reserved the maker's acceptance, so it wasn't an offer; the order was. The maker accepted by shipping (§ 2-206). The arbitration clause conflicts with the factory's forum clause, and ◆ under the majority knock-out rule both drop out.
A quote reserving acceptance of the buyer's order isn't an offer.
Under § 2-207(1), the invoice isn't a counter-offer unless expressly conditional.
Between merchants, additional terms may come in, but this one conflicts with an express term of the offer.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Who is the offeror decides the case

q: Owner orally grants Tenant, for $5,000 actually paid, a one-year option to buy the rented house for $250,000. Ten months later, Tenant gives written notice exercising the option. Owner refuses, pleading the Statute of Frauds. Tenant has paid rent as usual and made no improvements. What's Owner's best argument?
o: It's a land contract with no signed writing.
The option was revocable because it was oral.
The option lapsed after a reasonable time.
There was no consideration given for the option itself.
oe: Correct. A paid option is a real contract (§ 25), but a contract for the sale of an interest in land is within the Statute. Possession as a tenant paying rent, without improvements or payments toward the price, generally doesn't satisfy § 129.
Paid consideration makes it irrevocable regardless of form; the problem is the Statute.
It ran for one year, and Tenant exercised in month ten.
Tenant actually paid $5,000.

q: A town posts a notice in the town hall: “$10,000 to anyone who restores the courthouse clock to working order by July 4. No need to tell us in advance — just get it running.” Jo, a clockmaker, gets the town's permission to enter the tower and spends two weeks rebuilding the gears. With the job half done, the town posts a notice in the same place withdrawing the offer. Jo doesn't see it, finishes on July 1, and the clock runs. Can Jo recover?
o: Likely yes: she had begun the invited performance before the withdrawal.
No: the offer was withdrawn before she finished the job.
No: notices posted by a government are never offers.
Yes, because she never saw the withdrawal.
oe: Correct. A reward notice seeking a performance is an offer. Once Jo began the invited performance, an option contract arose (§ 45), so the town couldn't revoke, and she then completed performance. (◆ A public offer can generally be revoked by equally public notice, but not after performance has begun.)
The withdrawal came after she had begun performance, so § 45 made the offer irrevocable.
A notice seeking a specific performance, like a reward, can be an offer.
◆ A general offer can be revoked by comparable publicity even if she never saw it. The stronger ground is § 45.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Reward, revocation, and part performance

q: For years, a wholesale florist has shipped roses to a hotel each week; the hotel keeps any shipment it doesn't reject within two days and pays monthly. This week the florist calls and says, “Sending 2,000 roses at the usual $1 each,” then sends a signed confirmation. The hotel, a merchant buyer of flowers, says nothing for two weeks, then refuses the shipment and pleads § 2-201. What result?
o: The hotel is bound on both points.
The hotel wins: silence can't be acceptance, and there's no writing signed by the hotel.
The hotel wins: the merchant's confirmation rule doesn't apply to perishable goods.
The florist wins only for the roses the hotel actually used.
oe: Correct. Prior dealings made silence acceptance (§ 69(1)(c)). Between merchants, a confirmation not objected to in writing within 10 days satisfies § 2-201 against the recipient (§ 2-201(2)).
Both exceptions apply here.
There's no perishable-goods exception.
The whole shipment is covered.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Silent acceptance and the Statute

q: A seller under a fixed-price contract to supply a unique component tells its only buyer: “Pay 30% more or we stop shipping tomorrow.” The seller's costs haven't changed. The buyer, unable to source the part elsewhere in time to meet its own customer's deadline, agrees in writing under protest, then sues promptly after the final delivery to recover the increase. Which theories support the buyer?
o: Both good faith and economic duress.
Neither: under the UCC, modifications need no consideration.
Only the pre-existing duty rule.
Only duress, because good faith doesn't apply to price terms.
oe: Correct. Section 2-209(1) needs no consideration but requires good faith; extortion without a legitimate commercial reason fails (cmt. 2). The facts also track Austin Instrument: wrongful threat, no alternative, protest, and a prompt suit.
No consideration is needed, but good faith is, and duress is a separate defense.
That common-law rule doesn't govern goods modifications.
The good-faith test applies to any modification under § 2-209.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Modification under pressure

q: A startup orally promises a software engineer a two-year contract at $150,000 a year if she relocates from London to Austin. She sells her flat and moves. One month after she starts, the startup fires her and pleads the Statute of Frauds. A court applying § 139 finds her reliance substantial and foreseeable. What remedy is most consistent with § 139?
o: Enforcement as justice requires, perhaps reliance only.
Full expectation damages for two years as a matter of law.
Nothing, because a two-year contract is within the Statute.
Specific performance of the employment.
oe: Correct. Like § 90, § 139 makes the promise enforceable notwithstanding the Statute, but the remedy may be limited as justice requires.
The court may award expectation but isn't required to.
Section 139 is the exception that applies.
Courts don't order employment to continue.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Promise, reliance, and the one-year rule

q: A buyer signs a contract to buy “Lot 7” in a subdivision, believing it's the lakefront lot she walked with the seller's agent. Lot 7 is actually a lot across the road. The agent knew the buyer believed Lot 7 was the lakefront lot and said nothing. The buyer had no reason to know the true location. What's the buyer's strongest position?
o: A contract on her meaning, or rescission.
No contract: the parties attached different meanings to “Lot 7.”
She's bound to buy the lot across the road because she signed.
She can sue for deceit even if the agent didn't know her belief.
oe: Correct. Under § 20(2), when only one side knows of the other's meaning, the contract is formed on the innocent party's meaning. And under § 161(c), silence that would correct a mistake about the contents or effect of a writing equals an assertion, which supports rescission if material.
That's § 20(1), which applies only if neither or both knew.
The seller's side knew of her meaning.
Deceit requires scienter, and the facts say the agent knew.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Misunderstanding or misrepresentation?

q: A seller signs a written option reciting “for $10 paid,” giving a buyer 30 days to buy a car for its fair market value. The $10 is never paid. The seller revokes on day 5. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Binding under the R2d; revocable under Burgess.
Under both views, the option is binding because courts don't inquire into adequacy.
Under both views, the option fails because $10 is nominal.
The option is binding only if the buyer relied before day 5.
oe: Correct. Section 87(1)(a) honors a recital of purported consideration in a signed writing on fair terms within a reasonable time. Burgess treats an unpaid nominal recital as no option at all. Argue both.
Adequacy isn't the issue; whether any consideration was paid is.
Nominal consideration can support an option, and the R2d accepts the recital.
Reliance is a separate § 87(2) route; it isn't required under § 87(1)(a).

q: A software company ships a home user an unrequested upgrade disc with a note: “Install within 30 days and you agree to pay $49 and to our terms, including arbitration.” The user installs and uses the upgrade. Her state has no unordered-merchandise statute covering software. The company bills her $49. Which is the best analysis?
o: She's bound by exercising dominion, unless the terms are manifestly unreasonable.
She isn't bound because silence can never be acceptance.
She's bound to pay but not to arbitrate, because she isn't a merchant.
She isn't bound because unordered goods are always gifts.
oe: Correct. Section 69(2): an offeree who exercises dominion over offered property is bound by the offered terms unless manifestly unreasonable. Silence alone wouldn't bind her, but using the software is conduct.
She did more than stay silent; she used the property.
Section 2-207(2) governs additional terms in an acceptance. Here the terms are in the offer she accepted by dominion.
Only where a statute so provides.

q: Two sophisticated companies sign a letter of intent stating it is “non-binding” and that “no obligation arises until a definitive agreement is signed.” Relying on oral assurances that “the deal is basically done,” the buyer spends $2 million on due diligence. The seller walks away. The buyer sues for promissory estoppel. What's the likely result?
o: The buyer likely loses: its reliance wasn't reasonable.
The buyer wins: it spent $2 million in reliance.
The buyer wins: the letter of intent was a binding contract.
The buyer wins expectation damages for the lost deal.
oe: Correct. Promissory estoppel requires reasonable reliance on a clear promise (Garwood). Sophisticated parties who agreed nothing was binding until a definitive agreement face a high bar.
Reliance must be reasonable and on a definite promise.
It expressly said it wasn't.
There was no enforceable promise of the deal.

q: A seller of a rare guitar posts online: “Vintage 1959 guitar, $40,000. Serious buyers, email me to arrange a viewing.” A buyer mails a letter: “I accept. Check enclosed.” The next day, the seller sells the guitar to someone else. The buyer argues his letter formed a contract when he mailed it. What result?
o: No contract: the post was an invitation to negotiate.
A contract formed when the letter was mailed.
A contract formed when the seller received the check.
No contract, because guitars over $500 require a writing signed by the seller.
oe: Correct. The ad was an invitation to deal. It sought a viewing, not acceptance. The mailbox rule applies only to acceptances.
The mailbox rule needs an offer to accept.
Receiving the buyer's offer isn't accepting it.
The more basic problem is that there was no offer.
